items.title: Reservists lead first joint battlefield training exercise at Davis-Monthan
items.author: Courtesy
items.summary: Reservists from the 943d Security Forces Squadron led a first-of-its-kind joint-service battlefield training exercise Sept. 13, 2026, at Davis-Monthan Air Force Base.
items.body:
DAVIS-MONTHAN AIR FORCE BASE, Ariz. -- Reservists from the 943d Security Forces Squadron led a first-of-its-kind joint-service battlefield training exercise Sept. 13, 2026, at Davis-Monthan Air Force Base.

The event brought together Air Force Reserve, Navy Reserve, and active-duty Marine Corps personnel to practice working as one team in realistic field conditions. Participants included security forces, aircraft maintenance and medical specialists from the 943rd Security Forces Squadron, 943rd Maintenance Squadron, 943rd Critical Care Air Transport Team, Navy Reserve Center hospital corpsmen and master-at-arms and a Marine assigned to inspector-instructor duty at the Navy Reserve Center.

Throughout the exercise, teams faced a series of simulated combat scenarios designed to test communication, movement, security, medical care and casualty evacuation. The training supported Air Force Reserve priorities to modernize tactical units and improve the ability of different specialties and services to operate together. The exercise included five main events:

Mission briefing: Participants received a common mission plan and established shared radio procedures and command structure.

Combat patrol: Air Force, Navy, and Marine personnel moved together through Fire Base Elvis while practicing patrol formations, area security, and radio communication.

Emergency medical care: Teams treated simulated casualties using Tactical Combat Casualty Care techniques, including bleeding control and airway management.

Casualty evacuation: Personnel transported injured members by foot while maintaining security along the route.

Medical hand-off: Navy corpsmen transferred patients to Air Force critical-care transport personnel, simulating the transition from frontline treatment to advanced care during evacuation.

Senior enlisted leaders and officers observed the event, assessed performance, and documented lessons learned for future training.

The exercise was the first local event of its kind to combine these units in a single field training environment. By practicing together before a real-world deployment or emergency, the participating services strengthened their ability to communicate, respond quickly and provide care under demanding conditions.

items.title: NAVFAC Hawaii completes construction of new Military Working Dog Kennel at MCBH
items.author: Anna Marie G. Gonzales
items.summary: Naval Facilities Engineering Systems Command Hawaii (NAVFAC HI) completed construction of a new $8.3 million military working dog kennel at Marine Corps Base Hawaii (MCBH) with contractor Alan Shintani Inc., providing a modern facility to support military working dog operations and installation security.
items.body:
Naval Facilities Engineering Systems Command Hawaii (NAVFAC HI) completed construction of a new $8.3 million military working dog kennel at Marine Corps Base, Hawaii (MCBH) with contractor Alan Shintani Inc., providing a modern facility to support military working dog operations and installation security.

The P-955 Military Working Dog Kennel was commemorated during a maile lei untying ceremony Sept. 23 at MCBH, Kaneohe Bay, Hawaii.

Col. Steve Detrinis, commanding officer of MCBH, hosted the ceremony, which brought together base leadership, Provost Marshal’s Office personnel, military working dog handlers, NAVFAC HI personnel, contractors and project partners.

“It is a distinct honor to be here today on behalf of Naval Facilities Engineering Systems Command Hawaii to celebrate the completion of this outstanding and critical warfighting facility,” said Capt. Andrew Hunt, NAVFAC Hawaii executive director. “When we look at a military construction project, we see far more than the concrete and steel before us. We see a vital new capability — one that directly strengthens our warfighting readiness and enables critical teams for the missions ahead.”

The new kennel replaces an aging facility and provides military working dogs and their handlers with infrastructure designed to support their health, safety and readiness.

The 14-kennel facility includes individual indoor and outdoor working areas, veterinary and specialized food preparation rooms, slow-crank doors and overhead power washers.

NAVFAC Hawaii worked with MCBH’s kennel master, base veterinarian and Provost Marshal’s Office throughout the project to incorporate operational requirements into the facility’s design and construction.

“This kennel is an investment in our operational approach,” Detrinis said. “This new facility is a product of our priority to protect people and infrastructure.”

The project supports MCBH’s effort to modernize infrastructure and strengthen the installation as a resilient power projection platform in the Indo-Pacific.

NAVFAC Hawaii ROICC [resident officer in charge of construction] MCBH construction management team provided design and quality assurance for the project, working with contractor Alan Shintani Inc. and its subcontractors to complete construction.

“A project’s true performance, however, is measured not just by the final product, but by the teamwork it took to get there,” Hunt said. “The success we are celebrating today is a direct result of exceptional collaboration. This was a partnership in the truest sense of the word.”

The facility provides military working dog teams with an operating environment designed around their mission. Military working dogs provide specialized capabilities, including explosive and narcotics detection and patrol operations, supporting installation security and force protection.

Military working dogs have served alongside U.S. service members for more than a century. During World War II, Marine Corps war dog platoons deployed throughout the Pacific, where dogs helped detect ambushes, mines and concealed enemy positions.

The partnership between military working dogs and their handlers remains central to the mission.

“Where my dog goes, I go,” is a creed embraced by military working dog handlers that reflects the trust and shared responsibility between handler and dog.

“I hope this gives handler and dog alike the mission and operating platform that they can call home and that both are proud to operate from,” Hunt said.

The completion of P-955 demonstrates NAVFAC Hawaii’s role in providing infrastructure that supports Navy and Marine Corps readiness and mission requirements across the Indo-Pacific.

“May it serve you, our military working dogs, their handlers and our nation with distinction, steadfastness and unwavering loyalty for decades to come,” Hunt said.

items.title: Air Force, Industry Fears Continuing Resolution Could Hinder CCA Production
items.author: Steve Losey
items.summary: The Air Force’s emerging Collaborative Combat Aircraft program would suffer delays if Congress fails to pass a budget before the end of this calendar year, a top service official said Sept. 28. Brig. Gen. Timothy Helfrich, the portfolio acquisition executive... The post Air Force, Industry Fears Continuing Resolution Could Hinder CCA Production appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
The Air Force’s emerging Collaborative Combat Aircraft program would suffer delays if Congress fails to pass a budget before the end of this calendar year, a top service official said Sept. 28.

Brig. Gen. Timothy Helfrich, the portfolio acquisition executive for fighters and advanced aircraft, said the program is ready for production, but advancing to that next stage requires a new budget. “You can’t go do production without production funding,” he said during a Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies appearance. “So that does provide limitations on what we can execute.”

CCAs are the semi-autonomous drone fighters the Air Force believes can bolster its manned fighter force. The first two models—General Atomics Aeronautical Systems’ FQ-42A Vengeance and Anduril Systems’ FQ-44A Fury—are designed for air-to-air strike missions. The objective is for the compact uncrewed CCAs to cost less than $20 million apiece for the airframe, and to rapidly grow the force to include at least 500 in 2032, on its way to at least 1,000 later on.

Fiscal 2027 starts Oct. 1, but Congress failed to pass a budget before taking its reccess, instead passing a funding measure that extends until Dec. 11 appropriations at 2026 levels. Under such a continuing resolution, new programs, such as CCA production, are not authorized. If Congress fails to pass a budget the government could be forced to shut down. Congress could also vote to extend the CR for a month or more at that time.

Helfrich’s comments echoed concerns raised by Anduril officials at the Air & Space Forces Association’s Air, Space and Cyber conference in National Harbor, Md., Sept. 14.

Erin Simpson, Anduril’s vice president of strategy execution for air dominance and strike, told reporters in a briefing that the company has worked to get a head start on procurement, including by building a new Arsenal-1 factory in Columbus, Ohio, buying parts in advance, and producing prototype Fury CCAs.

“We will not have a cold start to [launch] production in ’27,” Simpson said. “We will have assets rolling through. That said, even a company like ours can only do so much without procurement dollars.”

When asked about the CR’s potential effect on General Atomics’ production, a company spokesman pointed to a Sept. 21 release that said it is taking on risk by self-funding some of the first FQ-42s, to keep the program moving forward while the Pentagon’s funding is worked out.

“Production of FQ-42 Vengeance is underway on company investment as government funding plans mature, with GA-ASI continuing its longstanding tradition of working at-risk with its own funds to support U.S. procurement planning and prevent delays in delivery,” General Atomics’ statement said. GA-ASI plans to build multiple fighters for its own company aircraft fleet, to invest in inventing new technologies that reduce risk and increase capabilities for its global customers.”

Helfrich said the Air Force’s upcoming Emerald Flag exercise in December at Eglin Air Force Base, Fla., will be a significant demonstration of how far CCAs have come. And it will further the work done by the Air Force’s Experimental Operations Unit to figure out how best to use CCAs in operational environments, and how to operate it under the Agile Combat Employment construct of flying aircraft out of dispersed, small and rough airfields in a future conflict.

“Setting up for Emerald Flag, it’s all hands on deck, but the EOU is central to making that happen,” Helfrich said. “They’re at the heart of taking a capability and making it into something that we can actually integrate into the Air Force.”

Both initial CCA models will fly at Emerald Flag alongside different manned fighters, he said, possibly with multiple CCAs flying at once.

The Air Force announced in July that Anduril’s Fury CCA had fired its first live missile in a test. General Atomics’ Vengeance will soon follow, Helfrich said. Helfrich indicated that test fire would likely happen before Emerald Flag.

General Atomics spokesman C. Mark Brinkley declined to say exactly when the first FQ-42A live-fire test may take place, saying only that it would happen by the end of the year.

Helfrich said the FQ-42A’s live-fire test will focus on more than just launching the missile, and will be a test run of the entire process for firing weapons with an autonomous system, while still keeping a human “on the loop.”

“The human has to make the decision to use lethal force, and then go and engage on that target,” Helfrich said. “So we’re talking more like. Kill chain than we are about [a standard weapon firing] exercise.”

items.title: Airmen, Guardians Told to Select Religion Code from New Consolidated List
items.author: Matthew Cox
items.summary: Active-Duty Airmen and Guardians have until mid-October to update their personnel records with their religious preference using the Pentagon’s new consolidated list of Religious Affiliation Codes, according to a recent Department of the Air Force announcement. The post Airmen, Guardians Told to Select Religion Code from New Consolidated List appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
Active-Duty Airmen and Guardians have until mid-October to update their personnel records with their religious preference using the Pentagon’s new consolidated list of Religious Affiliation Codes, according to a recent Department of the Air Force announcement.

The new list of codes—ordered by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth—slashed the number of religions specified in the Pentagon’s HR systems from more than 200 to roughly 30. Officials said in June that the consolidation was necessary to streamline the number of religious preferences for service members and shape the chaplain corps to support them.

The consolidation process collapsed roughly 170 denominations of Christianity down to 21 and includes widespread non-Christian religions such as Buddhism, Hindu, Islam, and Judaism, among other faiths. It removes Wicca, paganism, and other nontraditional faiths from the list, replacing them with an “Other Religious” category.

The department directs all Active-Duty members of the Air Force and Space Force to select their new Religious Affiliation Code in the Virtual Military Personnel Flight system and certify their record of emergency data is accurate by Oct. 16, the announcement states. Members of the Air Force Reserve and Air National Guard have until Nov. 9 to update their records.

“Transitioning to these standardized codes ensures our chaplain corps has the accurate demographic data they need to provide tailored resources and support to our service members, while continuing to respect their individual convictions,” Richard Anderson, assistant secretary of the Air Force for manpower and reserve affairs, said in the announcement.

Airmen and Guardians who fail to update their RAC before the deadline will have their records automatically updated to a selection that aligns with the new RAC list. For example, paganism would likely fall under the “Other Religions” category, according to an Air Force official.

Individual Airmen and Guardians, however, will not be limited by the new RAC list for the purposes of identifying their religious preference on the ID tags or “dog tags” they wear around their necks. The tags can be vital for helping chaplains determine the religious needs of service members wounded in battle.

Hegseth announced the effort to consolidate the list of religious preferences in a March 24 video on social media, calling the older list of Faith and Belief Codes “impractical and unusable.” Hegseth also directed chaplains to replace their rank insignia with their appropriate religious affiliation insignia in an effort to make them more approachable to younger service members. The announcement came six months after Hegseth singled out paganism in September 2025 because some troops have petitioned for religious exemptions so they could grow beards.

“If you want a beard, you can join Special Forces,” Heseth told hundreds of general officers at Quantico, Va., last Sept. 30. “If not, then shave. We don’t have a military full of Nordic pagans, but unfortunately, we have had leaders who either refuse to call BS and enforce standards, or leaders who felt like they were not allowed to enforce standards.”

Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell has argued the new consolidated RAC list is not intended to provide a list of “officially approved” religions. Rather it is “designed to allow chaplains to quickly look at the religious composition of their units and determine how they structure resources to best provide for warfighters of all faith groups,” Parnell wrote in a June 5 social media post.

The Pentagon did not provide the older list of Faith and Belief codes for comparison, but Airmen and Guardians can compare the 2026 codes list to an older list taken from a March 2017 memo from the Armed Forces Chaplains Board:

items.title: Space Force Interested in Commercial Antennas to Control Satellites
items.author: Greg Hadley
items.summary: The Space Force is starting a new competition to bolster its aging network of antennas that track and manage Pentagon and other U.S. government satellites—and this time, acquisition officials are open to leasing commercial systems or even paying for commercial antennas as a service. The post Space Force Interested in Commercial Antennas to Control Satellites appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
The Space Force is starting a new competition to bolster its network of antennas that track and manage Pentagon and other U.S. government satellites—and this time, acquisition officials are open to leasing commercial systems or even paying for commercial antennas as a service.

In a Sept. 24 notice, the Space Force and the Missile Defense Agency announced they are resetting the Satellite Communications Augmentation Resource program with a “Commercial Solutions Opening.” Instead of providing a list of detailed requirements, these openings define “areas of interest,” inviting vendors to pitch ideas based on commercially available technology.

The SCAR program is the Space Force’s effort to “revitalize” its Cold War-era Satellite Control Network, a collection of 19 antennas dispersed around the globe that track and maneuver satellites and collect data about their health and status. The service awarded and later canceled a $1.4 billion contract for Blue Halo, now part of AeroVironment, to build and deliver 12 multibeam, phased-array antennas for SCAR.

After cancelling that deal in March, officials explained they wanted to leverage commercial technology rather than acquire a bespoke, Space Force-centric design. This latest announcement offers more details on the approch, detailing three “areas of interest” for the SCAR program:

- A government-owned, contractor-operated model using commercial systems

- Long-term, exclusive government leases of commercially owned and operated systems

- “Antenna as a Service” giving the government access to commercial systems that could also be used by other customers

Each area of interest has benefits and drawbacks, the announcement states. Government-owned often means “bespoke technical solutions, Government-led maintenance,” and limited funding, officials wrote. Leasing or antenna-as-a-service carries security concerns, including “cyber risks that must be mitigated, such as multi-tenant data leakage, scheduling conflicts, and software interoperability bottlenecks.”

But the announcement lays out why Space Force leaders are eager to avoid rerunning the usual acquisition playbook.

“Space operations demand global, high-frequency satellite passes, yet owning and operating a globally distributed physical network is financially burdensome,” the announcement states. “Shifting to commercial ‘shared’ networks alleviates the need to establish dozens of Government-owned sites or dedicated leases.”

The current Satellite Control Network antennas can maintain contact with only one satellite at a time and not for very long. The network’s capacity is under strain as the Pentagon and other government agencies put up more and more spacecraft. According to a 2023 Government Accountability Office report, utilization rates have already been higher than the industry standard for the past decade, and Space Force leaders are expecting the number of satellites on orbit to greatly expand in the coming years.

Companies interested in SCAR have until Oct. 15 to submit white papers. The program office will then select one or more to move to a second phase of consideration.

items.title: For First Time, US F-35s Will Join Exercise in India
items.author: Greg Hadley
items.summary: Six U.S. Air Force F-35A fighters and 200-plus Airmen deployed to India on Sept. 26 for their first appearance in a large-scale exercise on Indian soil. The post For First Time, US F-35s Will Join Exercise in India appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
Six U.S. Air Force F-35A fighters and 200-plus Airmen deployed to India on Sept. 26 for their first appearance in a large-scale exercise on Indian soil.

Exercise Tarang Shakti will run from Sept. 26 to Oct. 12, according to the Indian Air Force, with eight countries contributing aircraft. First held in 2024, the exercise is India’s largest multinational aerial training event.

U.S. Ambassador to India Sergio Gor and Pacific Air Forces confirmed the arrival of the F-35s and released images of them at Jodhpur Air Force Station. The aircraft are from the 13th Fighter Squadron at Misawa Air Base, Japan.

This is the first time the USAF has deployed F-35s for an exercise in India, although USAF did previously display the Lightning II at Aero India, a large-scale air show. In 2024, the Air Force sent A-10s to Tarang Shakti in 2024, and USAF has sent F-15s and F-16s to participate in previous editions of Cope India, a major joint air combat exercise.

The U.S. and Indian air forces have built up their interaction in recent years. A B-1 bomber landed in India for the first time for Aero India in 2021, then returned for its first exercise at Cope India 2023. Last year, President Donald Trump suggested the U.S. might eventually sell F-35s to India, but little has been said on that topic since.

On the flip side of U.S.-India relations, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi has also worked to build ties with Russia and China. Modi met with Russia’s Vladimir Putin and Chinese Premier Xi Jinping earlier this month at the BRICS (Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa) summit, at which he stressed better relations with both Russia and China.

The Indian Air Force has an eclectic mix of aircraft, including indigenous HAL Tejas light combat aircraft, Russian Su-30s, French Rafales and Mirage 2000s, American C-17s, and more. Russia has also pitched its new Su-57 fighter to India—the Su-57 and F-35 were both at Aero India in 2025.

items.title: Not alone: Fort Sill summit strengthens connections before crisis
items.author: Chris Gardner
items.summary: Fort Sill’s Suicide Prevention and Holistic Health and Fitness Summit brought Soldiers, family members, leaders and installation organizations together Sept. 24 to strengthen awareness of suicide-prevention resources and protective factors. Through H2F classes, support agencies and personal stories, the event emphasized that Soldiers do not have to face stress or crisis alone and that connection, early intervention and access to resources can help before a crisis develops.
items.body:
FORT SILL, Okla. — Sometimes the first step toward getting help is simply finding a reason to start talking.

USO volunteer Linda Lettau has watched that happen with Molly, her certified therapy dog. Soldiers who initially say little will begin petting Molly, asking questions and, eventually, talking.

“I’ve sat with Soldiers, and they’re basically almost nonverbal when we start,” Lettau said. “We’ll talk, and they’ll start asking questions about the dog and start talking.”

That kind of connection, through a battle buddy, family member, leader, chaplain, counselor, volunteer or even a four-legged visitor, was at the heart of Fort Sill’s Suicide Prevention and Holistic Health and Fitness Summit Sept. 24.

The Army Substance Abuse Program hosted the summit with brigade H2F leads and organizations from across the installation. The event drew 285 attendees for classes, resources and conversations aimed not only at responding when someone is in crisis, but also at strengthening the factors that help people cope before they reach that point.

For Fort Sill, there are encouraging signs.

Tiffany Denard, an ASAP specialist, said Fort Sill has gone more than a year without a death by suicide and that suicide attempts have been trending downward. Soldiers continue to report suicidal thoughts, she said, but their willingness to speak up creates an opportunity for others to intervene and connect them with care.

“We have the ability to step in and support and provide the care and resources the individuals need,” Denard said.

The goal is to reach people even earlier.

Denard said there is rarely a single warning sign or cause behind someone reaching a crisis. Suicide prevention also means strengthening the relationships, habits and resources that help people manage stress and adversity.

“Protective factors are not just individual traits, but they are deeply social,” she said.

That idea helped bring suicide prevention and H2F together for the summit.

The Army’s H2F approach focuses on five readiness domains, physical, mental, spiritual, nutrition and sleep, recognizing that each can affect a Soldier’s overall well-being and ability to perform.

Sleep is one example. Denard said sleep problems affect about half of Fort Sill Soldiers, leaving many without the recovery they need to manage stress effectively. Three summit classes focused on sleep quality and routines that can help Soldiers recover and reset.

For Sgt. 1st Class Mumbi Williams, representing the Fort Sill SHARP Resource Center, the event also reinforced the connection between personal wellness and readiness.

Williams said learning about the organizations represented at the summit helped her consider ways to improve her own wellness so she can remain mission ready and better serve others in the Fort Sill community.

She also saw value in simply learning what is available.

Williams said Soldiers may be familiar with some resources but unaware of others, and she encouraged them to take what they learned back to their units and share it.

That matters because help does not have to begin in one particular office.

Fort Sill’s support network includes ASAP, the Employee Assistance Program, chaplains, Military and Family Life Counselors, behavioral health professionals and numerous other organizations. Because many services are confidential, Denard said there is no simple way to count everyone receiving assistance across the installation.

What matters, she said, is having multiple ways for people to find support.

Denard identified proactive leadership, community-wide accountability and integrated referral networks as central to Fort Sill’s prevention efforts. Soldiers also receive Ask, Care, Escort Suicide Intervention training, or ACE-SI, while ENGAGE Bystander Intervention Training is designed to address concerns such as stress, harmful behavior or harassment before situations worsen.

For Soldiers, the summit also offered an opportunity to think about how they respond to the pressures that come with Army life.

Pfc. Tagiilima Simeamativa Lefiti, a 13B cannon crewmember with the 428th Field Artillery Brigade, said the physical demands of her job made the summit’s nutrition and fitness information personally relevant.

But another session made her think differently about the pressure Soldiers can place on themselves when they struggle to meet a standard.

Instead of interpreting an area that needs improvement as something she cannot do, Lefiti said the session encouraged her to reframe the challenge and recognize that she does not have to solve it alone.

“I know I can do it,” Lefiti said. “I just need a team.”

That message extended beyond Soldiers.

Family member Amani Potter initially attended the summit for required training but stayed after discovering how much information and how many resources were available.

For Potter, one of the strongest lessons was the importance of sharing what someone is experiencing instead of withdrawing from others.

“When you’re isolated, it just attacks your mind,” Potter said.

The summit’s “Wall of Reasons to Stay” reinforced that message. Participants were invited to reflect on the people, relationships and other things that give their lives meaning.

Potter said people interact every day without necessarily knowing what someone else may be going through. His takeaway was to be genuine, consider others and remember that even a simple act of kindness can matter.

Lettau sees that connection in a different way with Molly.

She said Soldiers who have been separated from home during training sometimes tell her they have not seen their pets in months. Some become emotional while spending a few minutes petting Molly.

“They just love on her, and they’ll get teary-eyed,” Lettau said. “It really does have an impact.”

Lettau is quick to give Molly the credit.

“I just tell people Molly does the work, and I’m just legally somebody has to hold the leash,” she said.

The humor carries a larger point: Support can come from many places, and someone who is struggling does not have to know exactly which resource to call before asking for help.

Denard said anyone concerned about a Soldier, co-worker, friend or family member can begin with the same framework Soldiers learn through ACE: Ask, Care, Escort.

Check in. Listen. Show that the person matters. Then help connect that individual with the resource appropriate for the situation.

That might be a leader, chaplain, EAP professional, Military and Family Life Counselor, behavioral health provider, emergency department or the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline.

No one person is expected to diagnose the problem or have every answer.

Soldiers, family members, Army civilians and leaders who want more information about Fort Sill ASAP or the Suicide Prevention Program can call 520-725-7337 .

For Soldiers and leaders, that may be one of the summit’s most important messages: Strength is not measured by how much someone can carry alone. Sometimes readiness means recognizing when another person needs support, knowing where help is available and staying alongside them long enough to reach it.

And sometimes it means being willing to say what Lefiti did:

“I just need a team.”

HELP IS AVAILABLE: If you or someone you know is in crisis, contact the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline by calling or texting 988 , or chat online at 988lifeline.org . Help is confidential and free.

For more information about the Fort Sill Army Substance Abuse Program and Suicide Prevention Program , call 520-725-7337 .

items.title: More Than a Mission: Building Bonds Through Faith
items.author: SGT Samarion Hicks
items.summary: PORT MORESBY, Papua New Guinea — U.S. Army Chaplain Jon Knoedler, the senior Chaplain for the 8th Theater Sustainment Command, traveled to Port Moresby, Papua New Guinea (PNG), to engage with the local community and offer methods to improve ethical decision making and spiritual resiliency amongst community leaders.
items.body:
PORT MORESBY, Papua New Guinea — U.S. Army Chaplain Jon Knoedler, the senior Chaplain for the 8th Theater Sustainment Command, traveled to Port Moresby, Papua New Guinea (PNG), to engage with the local community and offer methods to improve ethical decision making and spiritual resiliency amongst community leaders.

“So here in PNG, religion brings an asymmetrical advantage, something that other near-peer threats don’t bring in, don’t have, and don’t encourage,” Knoedler said. “In fact, it’d be the opposite. So where they bring in a lot of money, we bring in what drives culture, which is religion.”

The request for chaplain support was identified by the Oceania Engagement Team (OET), a U.S. Army Pacific Civil Affairs Company deployed to PNG and throughout Oceania to conduct civil affairs and civil-military operations.

OETs operate in multiple countries within the Pacific, including PNG, Timor-Leste, Marshall Islands, Fiji, Micronesia, Palau, Tonga, Solomon Islands, Vanuatu, and Kiribati. The OETs maintain U.S. Army Pacific Command’s persistent presence in Oceania by working with regional partners in support of a free and open U.S. Pacific.

“We have a focus on religious and educational projects that allow the Papua New Guinean populace to get a glimpse of what the United States Army has to offer and how we can better bolster their abilities to do and achieve things in their religious and educational communities,” said Capt. Steven Riley, the Team Leader for OET-PNG.

In late September 2026, the Chaplain arrived and met with a Chaplain counterpart from the PNG Defense Force (PNGDF) to discuss how they could work together to train more Chaplains and give them tools to assist soldiers in spiritual and faith-based ways.

“We are currently going through different exercises and workshops where the Chaplain is able to speak with civil professionals that lead the local communities here in PNG,” said Riley. “We’re also meeting with PNGDF, PNG Correctional Services, as well as PNG Constabulary to provide them the ability to ethically lead and manage the status and position that they have, responsibly through faith.”

At Saint Joseph’s International Catholic Church, the Chaplain spoke with members of the congregation about what gives them life, what some of those killers of that life are, and how to use it practically with other people and themselves.

“For us to have these sessions with the U.S. Army Chaplain was an honor for us because it was our first experience,” said Paul Harricknen, the president of the Catholic Professionals Society of PNG. “It was very impressive, and we felt that the topics we covered, such as leadership, crisis management, and ethical leadership, were important because those are issues for us.”

With the intention of strengthening the culture within PNG and building spiritual resiliency, the Chaplain reached the hearts of the congregation and gave life to those who brought him life with the word of God.

items.title: Montford Point Retired Marine Henry B. Edwards Receives Congressional Gold Medal Award
items.author: LCpl Nalanie Davila
items.summary: NEW ORLEANS - More than eight decades after stepping forward to earn the title of United States Marine, Montford Point Marine Henry B. Edwards received recognition for a legacy that helped shape the Marine Corps for generations to come.
items.body:
NEW ORLEANS - More than eight decades after stepping forward to earn the title of United States Marine, Montford Point Marine Henry B. Edwards received recognition for a legacy that helped shape the Marine Corps for generations to come. Edwards, 97, was presented the Congressional Gold Medal by Maj. Gen. Douglas K. Clark, deputy commander, Marine Forces Reserve and Marine Forces South, during a ceremony at Bethel Ame Church in New Orleans on Sept. 27, 2026.

Edwards was born March 28, 1929, in Chickasaw, Alabama. After graduating from Mobile County Training School in Plateau, Alabama, in 1946, Edwards enlisted in the Marine Corps that same year. His path took him to Montford Point at Camp Lejeune, North Carolina, where he was among the approximately 20,000 African American men who trained between 1942 and 1949, becoming part of a generation whose service helped break racial barriers within the Marine Corps.

After completing training, Edwards served overseas in Saipan and San Juan, before being honorably discharged in 1947. Though his time in uniform was brief, his commitment to public service continued for decades. In 1948, Edwards enrolled at Southern University and A&M College in Baton Rouge, Louisiana, where he pledged to the Omega Psi Phi Fraternity, participated in the Honor Society Association and earned his degree in 1951.

Edwards later served as a supervisor at Brookley Air Force Base in Mobile, Alabama, an automotive repair instructor at Camp Lejeune, North Carolina, and as an automotive instructor at a vocational school back in Mobile. His career eventually led him to federal service with the U.S. Department of Labor, where his assignments took him to Dallas, New Orleans, Memphis, Tennessee, and Jackson, Mississippi, before retiring in 1987.

His dedication to selfless service also extended into his community and church. Edwards spent years serving in leadership roles at the Bethel African Methodist Episcopal Church in New Orleans and within the Ninth Episcopal District, as well as at Pine Grove AME Church in Mobile. In 1953, Edwards married Irma Frye Edwards. Their family grew across generations, and the young Marine who once arrived at Montford Point became a father, grandfather and great-grandfather of five. Nearly seven decades later, Edwards stood before another generation of Marines as Clark presented him the Congressional Gold Medal.

“There will be no discrimination, prejudice or immoral conduct in my organization,” Clark said. “You are a legacy, and we all thank you for your selfless service and the path you paved for the Marines who followed.”

This recognition represents more than a single moment in Edward's lifetime. His story spans from Montford Point to federal employment, faith, family and decades of community service. Serving as a reminder of a legacy of service across a lifetime.

items.title: Burlington wins $6.7M DoW grant for fire station
items.author: Lori McFate
items.summary: The planned facility, at 2100 N. Roosevelt Ave., directly supports the plant by stationing full-time heavy firefighting apparatus, advanced emergency response equipment and expanded staffing significantly closer to the installation's gates. The new facility will also handle residential and commercial calls in northern Burlington.
items.body: MIDDLETOWN, Iowa — The city of Burlington is receiving a grant of more than $6.7 million from the Department of War to construct a permanent fire station serving the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant. The planned facility, at 2100 N. Roosevelt Ave., directly supports the plant by stationing full-time heavy firefighting apparatus, advanced emergency response equipment and expanded staffing significantly closer to the installation's gates. The new facility will also handle residential and commercial calls in northern Burlington. The grant follows a formal endorsement by plant leadership during the federal fiscal 2026 application cycle. "Cultivating strong mutual aid partnerships is absolutely vital to our mission, our workforce, and our force protection posture," said Lt. Col. Daniel V. Nosse, commander of the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant. "As a critical node in our nation’s Organic Industrial Base, IAAAP produces quality medium- and large-caliber munitions essential to the Joint Force. Rapid, heavy emergency response capability is not just an operational asset, it is a life-safety imperative for our workforce and our surrounding communities." Currently, the ammunition plant's emergency services division operates with minimal staffing and relies on the Burlington Fire Department, the only full-time professional department in the immediate area, as its primary mutual aid partner for major emergencies, structural fires and multi-patient incidents. While a temporary facility operates about 4 miles from the installation, it also houses minimal staff. The permanent station will reduce heavy apparatus travel distance, cutting response times to the installation. Final grant agreements and project timelines will be coordinated between the city of Burlington and the Office of Local Defense Community Cooperation in the coming weeks. The funding is being awarded through the Office of Local Defense Community Cooperation’s Defense Community Infrastructure Program. The Defense Community Infrastructure Program is a competitive grant program administered by the Department of War’s Office of Local Defense Community Cooperation. It provides grant assistance to state and local governments to address physical infrastructure deficiencies that support military installations and improve the resilience and quality of life for service members and neighboring communities.

items.title: US Coast Guard Cutter Escanaba returns home to Portsmouth, Virginia, after seizing more than 2 million in illegal narcotics
items.author: PO2 Kate Kilroy
items.summary: PORTSMOUTH, Va. — The crew of the U.S. Coast Guard Cutter Escanaba (WMEC 907) returned to their home port in Portsmouth, Monday, following a 60-day deployment in the Windward Passage.
items.body: PORTSMOUTH, Va.— The crew of the U.S. Coast Guard Cutter Escanaba (WMEC 907) returned to their home port in Portsmouth, Monday, following a 60-day deployment in the Windward Passage. Operating under U.S. Coast Guard Atlantic Area and the Coast Guard's Southeast District, the Escanaba crew focused on the preservation of life at sea, the deterrence of unlawful maritime migration, and the denial of resources to transnational criminal organizations transiting the Caribbean Sea. On Aug. 29, Escanaba, assisted by an embarked law enforcement detachment from Tactical Law Enforcement Team (TACLET) Pacific, interdicted a vessel carrying approximately 2,082 pounds of marijuana, valued at more than $2.4 million. "I am so proud and fortunate to be a part of the crew of CGC Escanaba; the support and leadership of our command along with the tireless effort of the crew, made this interdiction happen," said Petty Officer 1st Class Douglas Strong, the deck watch officer who identified the smuggling vessel and served as the pursuit boat coxswain. "The excellent watch-standing and quick, crucial decisions enabled success.” In addition to the interdiction, Escanaba’s crew coordinated with the crew of the Coast Guard Cutter Richard Dixon (WPC 1113) to conduct an at-sea transfer of cocaine, weighing approximately 3,288 kilograms. Escanaba offloaded both illicit drug shipments in Port Everglades, Florida, advancing Coast Guard objectives to combat transnational criminal networks and enhance regional stability. During the patrol, Escanaba also conducted an underway replenishment with the commercial support vessel Homeland Security Cutter–Ocean (HSC-Ocean). The evolution provided the cutter with supplies needed to remain on station in the Windward Passage. "I am incredibly proud of the Escanaba crew for their exceptional performance and resilience throughout this high-tempo deployment," said Capt. Nicholas Seniuk, commanding officer of Escanaba. "Whether executing complex law enforcement operations with the support of our TACLET partners or coordinating vital mid-patrol logistics with the HSC-Ocean, the crew displayed the utmost professionalism. Their dedication directly prevented hazardous voyages and saved lives in the Windward Passage." Escanaba is a 270-foot Famous-class medium endurance cutter commissioned in 1987. The cutter's primary missions include search and rescue, law enforcement, maritime border security, and national defense operations throughout the Western Hemisphere.

items.title: Navigating the Disability Evaluation System: Hillary Charalambous’s Story
items.author: David Carrera
items.summary: Hillary Charalambous, a 2010 Naval Academy graduate and MH-60S Sierra helicopter pilot who deployed twice to the Arabian Gulf, was medically retired from the U.S. Navy in November 2022 at a 100% disability rating after recovering from a 9-hour craniotomy to remove a six-centimeter brain tumor. When a subsequent 18-month re-evaluation improperly reduced her rating to 60% despite no change in her medical condition, she sought help from the Navy JAG Corps’ Disability Evaluation System Counsel Progr
items.body: Navigating the Disability Evaluation System: Hillary Charalambous’s Story Hillary Charalambous graduated from the Naval Academy in 2010 and earned her wings in 2012 as an MH-60S Sierra helicopter pilot in the U.S. Navy. She deployed twice to Bahrain with Helicopter Sea Combat Squadron (HSC) 26, flying missions across the Arabian Gulf and Kuwait, as well as to various ships. The Diagnosis and Recovery Her military career took an unexpected turn when she woke up feeling as though her body was undergoing a “hard reset.” After medical scans at the hospital, doctors discovered a six-centimeter-long brain tumor. Hillary underwent a nine-hour, partially awake craniotomy, followed by intensive speech, occupational, and physical therapy to regain her independence and return home. Navigating DESCP Advocacy Following her diagnosis, Hillary entered the Medical Evaluation Board process through the Disability Evaluation System (DES) and was medically retired in November 2022 at a 100 percent disability rating. However, during an 18-month re-evaluation, her doctor documented that her condition remained unchanged, yet her rating was reduced from 100 percent to 60 percent. Seeking assistance, Hillary contacted the U.S. Navy JAG Corps’ Disability Evaluation System Counsel Program (DESCP) and was connected with Navy & Marine Corps Disability Attorney Don Hodgdon. With dedicated legal advocacy, Hodgdon guided her through the re-evaluation process, successfully restoring her rating to 100 percent. Hillary has deep gratitude for the DESCP, noting that the program made her feel supported as an individual rather than just a number. About the Disability Evaluation System Counsel Program (DESCP) As explained by disability attorney Roberta Hirsch, the U.S. Navy JAG Corps' DESCP provides dedicated legal support to wounded, ill, and injured service members navigating the military’s Integrated Disability Evaluation System and Medical Evaluation Board processes. Specialized disability attorneys are located at military medical treatment centers nationwide to assist service members and their families. For more information about the program, visit: https://www.jag.navy.mil/legal-services/descp/

items.title: Russia raises 2027 military spending by 27%, budget documents show
items.author: Darya Korsunskaya, Reuters
items.summary: Russia plans to spend 17.1 trillion roubles, or $202 billion, on defense in 2027, a 27% increase.
items.body:
Russia plans to spend 17.1 trillion roubles, or $202.6 billion, on defense in 2027, around 27% more than the 13.5 trillion roubles, or $159.8 billion, originally budgeted and the highest figure since the start of the war in Ukraine in 2022, government documents seen by Reuters showed on Monday.

Total defense spending will amount to 50 trillion roubles, or $591.7 billion, in the next three years, according to the documents. In 2026, the government planned to spend 12.1 trillion roubles on defense, but the actual amount is classified and will not be disclosed. Some military spending can also be accounted for in other parts of the budget.

The documents also showed the government raised its estimate for its 2026 budget deficit to 3.2% of gross domestic product, from 1.6% of GDP previously. Budget spending in 2026 will increase by 13.2% to 48.6 trillion roubles, or 20.9% of GDP.

The government is expected to submit the draft budget to parliament by Oct. 1. Last week, it announced plans for new tax hikes in 2027 to finance the growing deficit. The documents showed that a new windfall tax on metals and mining companies was expected to raise about 200 billion roubles, or $2.4 billion, annually.

The documents showed that in 2026 the government will increase its net borrowing plan by 26% to 5 trillion roubles and spend 459 billion roubles — about 11% of the liquid part of its National Wealth Fund — to reduce the deficit. It also cut the oil and gas revenue estimate for 2026 to 7.6 trillion roubles from 8.9 trillion roubles previously.

The documents showed that state debt is set to rise to 21.7% of GDP in 2027 from 19.9% of GDP in 2026, above the 20% level seen by the authorities as safe. Total borrowing in 2027 will increase by 43% to 7.7 trillion roubles.

Class VI material is ship’s store resale inventory intended to support Sailors’ personal demand needs while deployed. Class VI generally includes convenience and quality of life items, such as toiletries, snacks, beverages, and similar merchandise. The
items.body: Naval Supply Systems Command (NAVSUP) Fleet Logistics Center (FLC) Jacksonville personnel recently tested multiple methods to procure and deliver Class VI material to vessels operating throughout the U.S. Fourth Fleet area of responsibility (AOR). Class VI material is ship’s store resale inventory intended to support Sailors’ personal demand needs while deployed. Class VI generally includes convenience and quality of life items, such as toiletries, snacks, beverages, and similar merchandise. These items are distinct from repair parts, operational consumables, and mission equipment. Despite end-of-fiscal-year constraints and cost-saving measures, NAVSUP FLC Jacksonville remains committed to sustaining deployed warfighters. The effort demonstrated that deliberate planning, close coordination, and flexible transportation solutions can ensure Sailors receive authorized ship’s store merchandise in austere locations. “With limited Navy logistics infrastructure in the region, we needed to demonstrate that the Navy has the capability and capacity to provide class VI supplies across the region,” Robert Brunson, NAVSUP FLC Jacksonville Fleet Logistics Support Department deputy director, said. “Class VI items are essential to shipboard quality of life and morale.” For the testing Panama was selected as the best location in the region to receive the items. Other locations such as Naval Station Guantanamo Bay, Cuba and Puerto Rico were not viable due to time and distance for ships to conduct port visits. In the absence of Navy Exchange Command (NEXCOM) services within the Fourth Fleet AOR, the team tested three delivery methods during the past month. The first method involved ordering material through NEXCOM in Norfolk, Virginia; transporting it to Charleston, South Carolina; and loading it onto a military flight, space available, for delivery to Panama. The second method tested was shipping material from Puerto Rico through commercial air transportation, accepting longer lead times and potential customs delays in Panama. The last method involved NEXCOM placing a blanket order agreement with the Army and Air Force Exchange Service (AAFES) operation at Fort Buchanon, Puerto Rico and shipping the material to Panama via military airlift. Lt. Cmdr. Johnny Quintong, NAVSUP FLC Jacksonville operational logistics planner, supported coordination of cargo movement and flight onload from Puerto Rico to Panama during the testing and coordinated items for receipt, storage, and delivery to the USS Gridley (DDG-101). “The 4th Fleet is not an easy AOR, it’s very challenging,” Quintong said. “The biggest take away is to be able to provide full support to our customer no matter how, what, why, where, and when challenges arise, we must face them to maintain warfighter readiness in the 4th Fleet AOR.” Each method successfully delivered material to the customer while presenting distinct planning considerations. The Norfolk-to-Charleston process required extensive coordination among multiple organizations to determine feasibility, synchronize cargo movement, and align delivery with aircraft schedules. The commercial-air option increased shipping costs because of cargo weight and carrier fees, while also carrying out the potential for customs delays. The Puerto Rico AAFES and military-airlift option supported an emergent requirement but required the ordering unit to coordinate transportation to the airfield, cargo staging, and aircraft loading areas. The team also identified payment procedures as a critical component of the process. It was determined that vendor quotes must be obtained before the ordering unit can generate and submit the documentation required for payment. During end-of-fiscal-year closeout, the vendor’s requirement for immediate payment conflicted with the timeline for government commercial purchase card payment through NEXCOM. Aligning vendor-payment procedures with operational timelines will help prevent delays in future deliveries. “NEXCOM’s involvement in processing the order and arranging payment to AAFES in a time sensitive evolution were critical in meeting the deadline to load on to the supporting airlift mission,” Brunson said. The effort confirmed that several viable methods exist to deliver Class VI material to ships operating in remote locations. Airlift, early coordination, and clearly defined responsibilities among ordering units and supporting organizations remain essential to meeting customer requirements. “The Navy has flexibility to use various options to sustain ship operations,” Brunson said. “Availability of transportation will drive which option is used in the future.”

items.title: Massachusetts Guard, Paraguayan NCOs Build Trust in Leadership Exchange
items.author: TSgt Lauren Ogburn
items.summary: Sixty Paraguayan service members and senior NCOs from the Massachusetts National Guard gathered in Asunción, Sept. 15-18, for a leadership event that strengthened professional bonds and sets the framework for future exchanges under their 25-year State Partnership Program.
items.body:
ASUNCION, Paraguay -- Sixty members of the Paraguayan Armed Forces attended a non-commissioned officer professional development (NCOPD) event in partnership with the Massachusetts National Guard here, Sept. 15-18. The bilateral engagement capped more than three years of coordination and collaboration among senior enlisted leaders from Massachusetts and Paraguay. Organizers designed the multi-day event to build the essential leadership skills noncommissioned officers (NCO) need to guide their formations, support their leaders and care for their troops.

Senior NCOs from the Massachusetts National Guard gave presentations and facilitated discussion about motivation, stress management, change management and the important role of NCOs in the military. Throughout the engagement, participants and presenters shared experiences, discussed challenges and exchanged best practices for leading troops.

“For me, the most important and significant lesson on leadership was that of trust,” said Miguel Sanchez, an NCO in the Paraguayan Army. “Trust builds beyond a brotherhood; it builds to efficiently accomplish the mission. For me, this lesson touched me very deeply, because I see the real personal value that I have in my role.” By pairing presentations with open discussion entirely in Spanish, the event gave NCOs from both countries a chance to strengthen professional relationships.

U.S. Air Force Master Sgt. Brian Vargas, a cyber systems operations NCO assigned to the 102nd Intelligence Wing, said everyone who attended willingly participated and brought insightful stories and perspectives. “We had different career fields, from special forces and combat engineers to aircraft crew chiefs and engine mechanics. The different points of view made the discussions insightful and meaningful,” said Vargas.

The NCOPD initiative centers on the mutual objective of professionalizing the enlisted force and expanding NCO development across both partner nations. By focusing on decision making, troop welfare and leadership attributes and behaviors, the engagement aimed to systematically strengthen the capability and readiness of enlisted leaders. “Sharing military bonds is foundational to human relationships and leadership structures that a make a military unit effective,” said U.S. Army Master Sgt. Hercules Lobo, an infantry leader in the Massachusetts Army National Guard. “The NCOs bond together as the backbone of leadership by turning orders into tactical actions. They are the trainers and mentors to junior service members, guardians of the welfare of their soldiers, airmen and sailors and enforcers of standards to uphold discipline, traditions and daily military standards. NCOs are the primary architects of a strong military.”

For the presenters, the bilateral exchange also reinforced core military principles.

“What I took away was that this State Partnership relationship should be one of the top priorities for the Massachusetts National Guard,” said Vargas. “The Paraguayan military was so grateful in us being there, and I feel like we can help them grow even more. In collaborating with them, I myself am reinforcing the values instilled in me throughout my career and in my professional military education.”

The milestone engagement highlights the enduring partnership between Massachusetts and Paraguay through the Department of War National Guard Bureau State Partnership Program. Over 25 years, collaboration between the partner nations has continuously evolved to address modern security challenges and meet the strategic objectives of Massachusetts, Paraguay and U.S. Southern Command.

Planning is already underway for future State Partnership Program NCOPD exchanges. This first NCOPD engagement establishes the framework for subsequent joint training events, aligned with the long-term bilateral security cooperation roadmap between Massachusetts and Paraguay.

items.title: Czech President visits Nebraska National Guard headquarters for discussions on Nebraska Guard’s 33-year partnership with Czech Armed Forces
items.author: Kevin Hynes
items.summary: LINCOLN, Neb. – History was made at the Nebraska National Guard air base in Lincoln, Nebraska, on Thursday, Sept. 24, 2026, when Nebraska Lt. Gov. Joe Kelly, Maj. Gen. Craig Strong, Nebraska adjutant general, and other senior Nebraska National Guard leaders, Soldiers and Airmen welcomed Czech President Petr Pavel to the Joint Force Headquarters for discussions on the Nebraska Guard’s 33-year-old relationship with the Czech Armed Forces. It is believed to be the first time in the history of the N
items.body: LINCOLN, Neb. – History was made at the Nebraska National Guard air base in Lincoln, Nebraska, on Thursday, Sept. 24, 2026, when Nebraska Lt. Gov. Joe Kelly, Maj. Gen. Craig Strong, Nebraska adjutant general, and other senior Nebraska National Guard leaders, Soldiers and Airmen welcomed Czech President Petr Pavel to the Joint Force Headquarters for discussions on the Nebraska Guard’s 33-year-old relationship with the Czech Armed Forces. It is believed to be the first time in the history of the Nebraska National Guard that the organization has hosted a head of state. “This was truly a monumental event for the Nebraska National Guard,” said Maj. Gen. Craig Strong. “After 33 years of partnering with the Czech Armed Forces and working together to address the many common challenges we face in the world, to have the actual Czech head of state visit us here in Nebraska was such an honor.” President Pavel was accompanied by Czech Ambassador to the United States Jakub Kulhanek, Czech diplomats, military leaders, governmental delegates, and members of the Czech media. “We are so pleased to have the President with us today,” said Nebraska Lt. Gov. Kelly during an official welcome to the Joint Force Headquarters witnessed by more than 100 Nebraska Soldiers, Airmen and civilian employees who lined the JFHQ’s three balconies. “I think if we were to go around and have everyone in this entire building tell us what their family heritage is, I suspect that one out of every three -- if not more -- would be of strong Czech heritage.” “The bonds are so great. The bonds have been very strong here recently with the Nebraska National Guard…,” Kelly added. “We are lucky to have you here for a few days. And we hope you enjoy it.” Historically, Czech roots run deep in Nebraska, which has the highest percentage of citizens, per-capita, who claim Czech as their heritage. That heritage was part of the reason why Nebraska and Texas were chosen to form a partnership with the Czech Armed Forces in 1993 through the State Partnership Program. Today, the Nebraska-Texas-Czech Republic partnership remains the only tri-lateral State Partnership Program effort in Europe. President Pavel said he was excited to visit the Nebraska National Guard, adding that the welcome he received at the Joint Force Headquarters rivaled the farewell he was given when he left NATO after having served for three years as the chairman of the NATO Military Committee. “But this is much better because it is a welcome. And it is a welcome in a country that is special to us… we feel here like it is our home,” said President Pavel. “So, thank you for this welcome. We look forward to hearing about our special relationship and seeing what you do.” During the two-hour visit, President Pavel received briefings on the Nebraska National Guard’s most recent engagements with the Czech Armed Forces along with information on planned future collaborations. He also learned more about how members of the Czech Armed Forces and the Nebraska National Guard are training together in such areas as cyber defense and aerial refueling. Following the briefings, President Pavel and the delegation toured a Nebraska Air National Guard KC-135R Stratotanker assigned to the Lincoln-based 155th Air Refueling Wing, as well as two Nebraska Army National Guard helicopters assigned to the Guard’s Army Aviation Support Facility No. 1 in Lincoln. Strong said the visit helped highlight the importance of the work that members of the Nebraska Army and Air National Guard are continuing to do with the Czech Armed Forces. “This was an extremely important event because it gave us an opportunity to celebrate the successes that we have had over the decades of our relationship with the Czechs while also reaffirming our commitment to the future,” Strong said. “We all know that we are facing an increasingly challenging and volatile world. As we work with the Czech Armed Forces and continue to learn from each other, we are helping each other build the capabilities that we need to best serve the citizens of our nations. We are clearly stronger together.” “Relationships are driven by shared commitments and shared motivations,” Strong said. “This visit gave us the opportunity to reaffirm that we are committed and motivated to continue to evolve our partnership with the Czechs, which has been built upon a spirit of trust, respect and shared values.” Later, President Pavel commented on the engagement in a social media post. “The Czech army has been cooperating with the local National Guard for more than 30 years,” Pavel’s post read. “During this time, our partnership has expanded to a number of areas. Currently, we are focusing, for example, on training our pilots or exercises in cyber defense.” “The surprising information for me was that every fifth member of the local National Guard has Czech roots,” Pavel continued. “I appreciate that our partnership has not only been maintained over the years, but continues to bring benefits to both parties.”

items.title: Software Deals Move Mobility Fleet Toward Common Operating Picture with Real-Time Data
items.author: Todd South
items.summary: A recent $21 million contract award to three software companies could give the Air Force’s airlift and tanker units real-time software updates in degraded environments, including aircraft fuel, logistics, and other mobility fleet data. The post Software Deals Move Mobility Fleet Toward Common Operating Picture with Real-Time Data appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
A recent $21 million contract award to three software companies could give the Air Force’s airlift and tanker units real-time software updates in degraded environments, including aircraft fuel, logistics, and other mobility fleet data.

The Defense Innovation Unit and Air Mobility Command announced Sept. 15 they have awarded deals to Defense Unicorns, Stator Integration Labs, and Air Space Intelligence, each providing different tools to move the prototype software to production and deployment across AMC platforms.

The effort is under the umbrella of AMC’s Open Mission Engine program. Dubbed OMEN, the program is aimed at giving aircrews and mobility commanders better real-time information in denied, degraded, intermittent, and limited environments.

An AMC spokesperson told Air & Space Forces Magazine that the program seeks to have “present, current, and usable” aircrew mission software without a reach back or needing to connect to ground networks or cloud infrastructure to obtain the necessary update.

The program is still in its prototype phase, the AMC spokesperson wrote in an email, so they could not share initial and full operational capability timelines.

Officials have described OMEN as creating a “common operating picture” for mobility forces that have long lacked sophisticated connectivity. Using edge computing, the system will be able to track fuel, deliver software, and fuse data to create that common operating picture across the fleet, which will then load into aircraft cockpits and tablets.

Defense Unicorns CEO and cofounder Robert Slaughter told Air & Space Forces Magazine that’s “what makes OMEN special.”

“There’s a lot of different AMC assets, and they all need a common operating picture,” Slaughter said.

A former Air Force major, Slaughter explained that OMEN will fuse data across multiple inputs to give each user a clear understanding of what’s happening where and when.

“I think the biggest thing is: how do you do that on your worst day, and I think that’s key. How do you get software delivery done?” Slaughter said. “Accelerate the speed of software delivery on the nation’s worst day, and that’s what OMEN’s ultimately all about.”

The goal, Slaughter said, is to get on-demand software updates in the users’ hands.

“That’s measured in hours, not months or weeks,” he said. “That is a gnarly problem.”

Mark Lepczyk, Air Space Intelligence’s vice president of defense, says that as things stand, mobility crews wind up “pulling numbers from separate systems and reconciling them while the situation keeps evolving,”

“Under DIU’s OMEN program we’re reading crucial data like fuel state directly from the aircraft, fusing it on the same screen with the threats, the weather, and mission details, and offering optimal course of action recommendations, so the crew can now make accurate decisions at machine speed,” Lepczyk wrote in an email.

ASI’s application, which creates the common operating picture via data fusion tech provided by Stator Integration Labs, runs on a tablet that aircrews currently carry, Lepczyk said.

“The aircraft and the command center are working from identical information. It connects to existing Air Force systems, shared data services, and beyond-line-of-sight connectivity. A traditional operating picture tells you what is happening right now,” Lepczyk wrote. “Ours projects forward, so if weather suddenly shifts 300 miles ahead, the crew immediately understands all impacts and options to mitigate.”

The OMEN software assesses the “ripple effect” of any disruption to fuel, timing, or mission objectives and then gives the user “executable options” to replan quickly, Lepczyk wrote.

“We configured our solution assuming that any network can fail. Data can be cached locally, and the applications intuitively cue the crew if any information is degraded or stale,” he wrote.

Finding the Tools

DIU sought a software solution with both open-source protocols and a purpose-built capability stack tailored to OMEN’s needs, , unit spokesperson Caroline Thompson told Air & Space Forces Magazine in an email.

The unit works with military organizations such as Air Mobility Command and industry vendors as a kind of middleman, finding the right prototype solutions to military problems.

OMEN fleet software is part of a larger DIU effort to get quickly updatable and upgradable software in action across all Pentagon entities, Thompson wrote.

“The OMEN project exemplifies DIU’s strategy to bridge this gap,” she wrote. “By establishing an air-gapped-native fleet management layer, OMEN is building a repeatable framework to push software updates and AI capabilities directly onto operational aircraft. This project provides Air Mobility Command with a scalable blueprint to keep tactical edge software current and mission-ready.”

Delayed software impacts are felt across the fleet.

“This agility is key because software is only useful if it can be accessed and updated in the environments where it is required, in this case, on aircraft in austere locations or at 35,000 feet in the air,” Thompson wrote.

Defense Unicorns’ Unified Defense Stack-Fleet software is what Airmen will be using through the OMEN program. Components of UDS software have been used to upgrade F-22s, F-16s, and C-17s.

Slaughter, who deployed as an Airman with AMC assets, is keenly aware of what delayed software updates can do to a fleet. Often, software updates on legacy platforms can be a depot-maintenance level task.

“The jet not only goes through a maintenance period on the flight line, but the jet has to fly somewhere and be grounded completely out of the fight,” Slaughter said. “That is huge. I mean, I have vulnerabilities in the system, and I need to patch these. Imagine the entire fleet saying, ‘Hey, all of you have to go to depot-level maintenance, and it’s going to take several days or a week per plane’…You literally couldn’t fight and win wars with that posture.”

While Defense Unicorns’ UDS software will run on large platforms such as airlift assets and tankers, the software can be trimmed down for fighters and even drones, Slaughter said.

And while contractors are running the software updates in the prototype phase for OMEN, Airmen will be taking the reins once it reaches the production phase, Slaughter said.

items.title: From Orbit to Canopy: Guardians explore another frontier in Jungle Operations Training Course- Panama
items.author: SGT Alyssa Norton
items.summary: Maj. Alyson Gleason, assigned to United States Space Force Headquarters, and Capt. Stephen Brown, assigned to 392nd Combat Training Squadron, became the first U.S. Space Force members to complete the Jungle Operations Training Course-Panama, Sept. 25, 2026, at Aeronaval Base Cristóbal Colón.
items.body: AERONAVAL BASE CRISTÓBAL COLÓN, PANAMA (Sept. 25, 2026) – Maj. Alyson Gleason, assigned to United States Space Force Headquarters, and Capt. Stephen Brown, assigned to 392nd Combat Training Squadron, became the first U.S. Space Force members to complete the Jungle Operations Training Course-Panama, Sept. 25, 2026, at Aeronaval Base Cristóbal Colón. The 18 day training course placed the Guardians alongside U.S. Army Soldiers and Panamanian partner forces in the jungle of Panama where they were required to learn survival skills such as moving tactically, finding food and operating as a multinational team in the dense jungle environment. Some of the obstacles candidates of JOTC-P have to face are a 5k run, a combat water survival assessment, a knots test and a culminating event testing everything they learn in the course. “I’m always interested in challenging myself and the jungle is a beast that we don’t get to tackle very often as Space Force Officers,” said Gleason. “I saw the opportunity, I wanted the chance to work with the Army and the Panamanian partners down here, and I thought this would be a unique place to challenge myself.” For Guardians, whose main priority is space domain, JOTC-P provides a different environment then they would typically operate in. The Guardians' participation also reflects the expanding opportunities for members of the Space Force to train with other military services and partner nations. Guardians furthering their training outside of their typical job scope creates a stronger organization overall, for Space Force and the U.S. Military as a whole. “I feel grateful for coming here to the jungle, because I try to go through every experience I can,” said Brown. “Not everybody is going to get the opportunity, so when that door opens I think you should always take it.” JOTC-P was established as part of a broader U.S.-Panama effort to strengthen security cooperation and interoperability. The course has brought together members of the Army, Marine Corps, Air Force, Space Force and Panamanian partner forces since its launch. Guardians going through the course is not only a success for Space Force, but for JOTC-P as the course grows in its participation creating stronger, more capable forces across the two nations. “I think it’s something that if any Space Force person wanted to challenge themselves physically or mentally and get an opportunity to work with the other services this is the place I would do it,” said Gleason. “ It was incredible.”

items.title: USS James E. Williams (DDG 95) Hosts USS Robert H. McCard Alumni Association for Warship Tour
items.author: PO2 Oscar Pichardo
items.summary: NAVAL STATION NORFOLK, Va. (Sept. 18, 2026) — The Arleigh Burke-class guided-missile destroyer USS James E. Williams (DDG 95) hosted members of the USS Robert H. McCard Alumni Association for a warship tour today, allowing the veterans to interact with Sailors and observe modern surface fleet capabilities.
items.body:
NAVAL STATION NORFOLK, Va. (Sept. 18, 2026) — The Arleigh Burke-class guided-missile destroyer USS James E. Williams (DDG 95) hosted members of the USS Robert H. McCard Alumni Association for a warship tour today, allowing the veterans to interact with Sailors and observe modern surface fleet capabilities.

During the shipboard visit, Williams Sailors conducted a walkthrough of the ship's hangar bay, demonstrated the mechanics of the Mark 45 5-inch gun, and discussed the daily realities of modern shipboard life. The tour provided a direct, face-to-face opportunity to strengthen the connection between active-duty personnel and veterans who operated in a vastly different technological era.

“For many of us, it’s new Navy, old Navy,” said Monny Hanna, CEO of the USS Robert H. McCard Alumni Association. “To see the contrast between where the Navy was and where it is today, with its sailors, its fleet, its ships and things like that, it’s just an eye-opening experience for many of our guests that attend our reunions and visit with the ships.”

While the McCard veterans once stood watch on a steam-powered destroyer, the crew of the Williams demonstrated how today’s surface warriors command gas-turbine engines, the Aegis Combat System, and the Mark 41 Vertical Launching System to defend the fleet.

“I just like meeting new people,” said Ensign Matthew Raiche. “I like to see the faces of people who have served in the past, hear their stories, learn what they served on and what the life of the Navy was like for them.”

By opening its brow to the alumni association, the Williams reinforced the timeless maritime bond that unites all generations of surface warriors, deepening the crew’s pride in their heritage while providing the visitors with an up-close look at the modern fleet.

“What is so great about this interaction with the guys is seeing their spirit and their support to the Navy as we did when we did our service time,” said Hanna. “It’s good to see that interaction and that they want to have with us, to allow us to come aboard and do the tours.” “I think it allows us to interact more on a more personal level, to kind of foster a relationship and garner rapport with one another, which makes it easier for us to relate to each other,” said Raiche.

“We so appreciate the camaraderie that they give when they bring us on board and let us tour the ship,” said Hanna.

The McCard, commissioned in 1945, carried the legacy of Marine Corps Gunnery Sgt. Robert H. McCard, who posthumously received the Medal of Honor during the Battle of Saipan. Following 35 years of distinguished service spanning the Korean War, the Cuban Missile Crisis, and the Vietnam War, the Navy decommissioned the destroyer in 1980 and transferred her to the Turkish Navy, where she served as TCG Kılıç Ali Paşa (D-349) until her final retirement in 1998. Hanna noted that the alumni association plans reunions and tours around the country to see how the sea service has changed since their time on active duty.

USS James E. Williams (DDG 95) is an Arleigh Burke-class guided-missile destroyer designed to provide advanced defensive and offensive capabilities as part of the Navy’s surface force.

items.title: EU nails down five defense priority areas to channel common spending
items.author: Rudy Ruitenberg
items.summary: Drones, counter-drone tech, air defense, seabed defense and eastern flank protection top the EU's list of desired capability areas.
items.body:
PARIS — European Union member states approved five projects for joint defense-industrial investment in priority areas including drones and counter-drone systems as well as air and missile defense, part of efforts to encourage more cooperation on defense spending and avoid overlap in the 27-nation bloc.

The five projects approved on Monday are now eligible for EU funding via the €1.5 billion (US$1.7 billion) European Defence Industry Program, the Council of the EU, which acts as the bloc’s co-legislator, said in a statement. The other selected projects are in the areas of maritime and seabed defense, space, and protection of Europe’s eastern flank.

The European Commission has allocated €325 million for European defense projects of common interest, or EDPCIs in EU lingo, as part of EDIP. While the commission has been pushing to reduce fragmentation in Europe’s defense industry, cooperation between member states has been challenging due to competing industrial interests, illustrated by the recent breakdown of a French-German project to develop a sixth-generation fighter jet.

“These pan-European projects will make a difference for our EU member states’ armed forces, for Ukraine and for our security as a whole,” European Commissioner for Defence Andrius Kubilius said in a post on the social-media network X, formerly Twitter.

He called the approval of the five projects of common interest a “major breakthrough” that will close critical capability gaps in the EU, with an “envisaged funding ambition” of around €190 billion by 2036.

The EDPCIs are large-scale projects that give member states a framework to cooperate on major defense initiatives that would be too large or complex for individual countries to tackle on their own, according to the commission. The projects are designed to extend beyond the current EDIP funding period, which runs through 2027.

The EU’s executive arm will now work with member states to implement the projects and monitor their progress, and also expects to provide financial support, it said in a separate statement on Monday. On average, 18 EU countries participate in each project, with Ukraine part of four of the five projects, the commission said.

The project on drone and counter-drone defense, with the acronym Decoder, unites most EU member states as well as Norway and Ukraine, according to a commission fact sheet. The indicative overall investment is in the range of €3.5 billion to €5 billion by 2033.

The integrated maritime and seabed defense project, or IMSD, has an indicated investment envelope of €43 billion to €72 billion by 2045, while indicative overall spending under consideration for the space project amounts to €24 billion by 2034.

Investment in the EU Federated Air and Missile Defence project, or EU-FIAMD, which includes an early warning element, could be anywhere between €55 billion and €80 billion by 2040, according to the commission fact sheet.

The Eastern Flank Watch project, which aims to strengthen security on the EU’s eastern border through “a comprehensive multi-domain effort,” with participation from 12 EU members as well as Norway and Ukraine, is indicated to result in between €60 billion and €100 billion of investments by 2036.

Rudy Ruitenberg is a Europe correspondent for Defense News. He started his career at Bloomberg News and has experience reporting on technology, commodity markets and politics.
