items.title: Evaluating the UK Government’s 10-year drug strategy
items.author: Carol Black
items.summary: Dame Carol Black, Lucy Strang, and Jennifer Newbould discuss RAND Europe’s evaluation of the first three years of implementation of the Treatment and Recovery Portfolio as part of the UK government’s 10-year drug strategy, From Harm to Hope.
items.body:
D-SITAR Methods Report

Apr 22, 2026

The captions for this video are auto-generated and have not been edited.

VideoPublished Sep 28, 2026

Dame Carol Black, Lucy Strang, and Jennifer Newbould discuss RAND Europe’s evaluation of the first three years of implementation of the Treatment and Recovery Portfolio as part of the UK government’s 10-year drug strategy. While the funding has been a welcome boost and there is wide support for the Portfolio’s aims, it has not yet achieved a world-class treatment system and a whole-system approach to alcohol and/or other drugs.

Dame Carol Black

It seems to me it's extremely important - I know there are lots of other very, very important things going on - but if you want better health and you want a safer society, you need to pay attention to drugs.

In 2021, drug-related deaths in the UK were the highest ever recorded. Dame Carol Black's independent review of drugs found that drugs cost an estimated £19bn to society annually and that long-term cuts in funding have led to a decline in skills, expertise and capacity in the treatment and recovery system.

My review of drugs was commissioned by the then Home Secretary who was Sajid Javid and he asked me to do it in two parts. The first part was to really look at the evidence of where we were with the drug scene and with addiction. Wherever you looked, it didn't matter which part of the drug agenda you looked at, we were in a bad place.

In response to the issue, the UK government published their 10-year drug strategy From Harm to Hope. This strategy included an additional £780m in funding over three years for the treatment and recovery system.

So over the past two-and-a-half years, RAND Europe and our partners have evaluated the first three years of the drug strategy's Treatment and Recovery Portfolio implementation in England. We evaluated the Portfolio as a whole, as well as focusing in on five priority areas which are the housing support grant, efforts to improve the treatment and recovery workforce, lived-experience recovery organisations, the integration of mental and physical health services and the provision of depot buprenorphine, which is a long-lasting medication used for opioid substitution therapy in the recovery process. So the workforce within the treatment and recovery sector was obviously a key priority of this additional investment. There was a widespread recognition that, after years of disinvestment, the state of the workforce had been depleted and it was a real challenge to build that up over time, specifically within the planned timelines of the Portfolio.

Our findings suggest that it's not necessarily the nature of the work that leads people to leave the sector, but other factors such as salary levels, job security, workload and the availability of resources. All these things are amenable to change and are what ultimately affect people's desire to continue in the treatment and recovery sector.

Another key priority of the Treatment and Recovery Portfolio was to improve mental and physical health service integration. So it's really critical for people who use treatment and recovery services to also have really well-integrated support from both mental and physical health services. This is because a lot of their needs are also extending to other mental health challenges or physical health needs and we do find that these individuals can often fall through the cracks between these services.

So we've now got three more years of money. And if I had to concentrate now it would be on absolutely addressing the quality issue: the quality of the workforce, the quality of what is done in the treatment areas really being more sophisticated and person-centred about delivery.

What we found through our evaluations was a few really important steps that the government should take in ensuring that the Treatment and Recovery Portfolio meets its intended aims and continues to provide really good outcomes for people who are using these services and for people who are working in the sector. First of all, we recommended that the government continue to provide more funding security to really ensure that the full 10 years of the Portfolio will be recognised and realised.

So the funding was well received, but in many areas people felt that it just replaced years of disinvestment. If we don't invest in people who use drugs and alcohol now, the problem will only get larger in the future.

We also really emphasised the importance of continuing to make progress with mental and physical health service integration to ensure that people who are using these services have all their needs addressed in a really collaborative and cohesive way.

We have failed so far to get drug addiction considered a chronic health condition and given the parity of a health condition. We haven't succeeded to improve the physical complications that drug-dependent people suffer from.

We also found that there is more work to be done in ensuring a whole-system approach to dealing with drug issues. So that involves work and collaboration across multiple sectors including health, education, employment, criminal justice and so on.

I would say please empower your local delivery services to be brave, to be less bureaucratic and to deliver a person-centred service. These are individuals with complex problems and they needed not to be treated as a number, a form-filling exercise. They need to be treated as a person with a chronic health condition, given some choice and able to go along a journey which will lead to recovery.

items.title: Ministry of Defence Police: misconduct hearings
items.summary: Find out about misconduct hearings involving Ministry of Defence Police (MDP) officers and how to attend these public hearings.
items.body:
To increase openness and transparency in the MDP (and the police service in general), misconduct hearings, special case hearings and police appeals tribunals, involving Police Officers, are held in public.

Misconduct hearings deal with allegations of gross misconduct committed by MDP officers on or off duty. Gross misconduct is defined as ‘a breach of the police standards of professional behaviour ( PSPB )’ that is so serious as to justify dismissal’. Misconduct hearings form part of the disciplinary process and are not criminal proceedings.

Accelerated Misconduct Hearings

Accelerated Misconduct Hearings take place when the investigation of allegations of Gross Misconduct, committed by MDP officers on or off duty, identifies that special conditions, such as the following are satisfied:

that there is sufficient evidence, in the form of written statements or other documents, to establish on the balance of probabilities that the conduct of the officer concerned constitutes Gross Misconduct

it is in the public interest for the officer concerned to cease to be a member of the MDP without delay

Police Appeals Tribunals

Police Appeals Tribunals deal with appeals submitted by MDP officers, against the findings and/or the outcomes of misconduct hearings (including accelerated misconduct hearings), under the MDP Conduct Regulations, or stage 3 meetings under the Performance Regulations.

The decision to hold misconduct hearings and police appeals tribunals in public was announced by the Home Secretary in 2015. The Ministry of Defence Police followed suit in March 2017 by amendments to the Ministry of Defence Police conduct (2015) and performance (2012) regulations, and by subsequent revision of those Regulations into the new Ministry of Defence Police (Conduct, Performance and Appeals Tribunals) Regulations 2020, which came into effect for all cases assessed as Gross Misconduct after 2 November 2020.

This change of legislation does not affect misconduct meetings, where a breach of PSPB does not amount to gross misconduct. These proceedings will be held in private and the public have no right to observe (except in the case of a complainant or the commission^, where appropriate).

^Director General (IOPC) or Ombudsman (NI) if they conducted or directed the investigation.

What happens at a misconduct hearing

At a misconduct hearing the facts are heard by a panel, often with the help of witnesses, to enable a finding to be made. If an officer is found to have committed misconduct or gross misconduct, depending on the circumstances, the available outcomes are:

written warning (only if misconduct only found)

final written warning

reduction in rank

dismissal without notice

What happens at an Accelerated Misconduct Hearing

An accelerated hearing is heard by the Chief Constable. Due to the evidence being incontrovertible there is no requirement for any witness attendance. If an officer is found to have committed gross misconduct, the available outcomes are:

What happens at a Police Appeals Tribunal

Police appeals tribunals are heard by a panel chaired by a person nominated by the Lord Chancellor who satisfies the judicial appointment criteria. The tribunal determines whether the ‘grounds of appeal’ on which the appellant relies, have been made out. On the determination of an appeal, a tribunal may make an order dealing with the appellant in any way in which they could have been dealt with at the original hearing.

Attending a misconduct hearing

Any member of the public or press can request to attend a misconduct hearing, provided that they are aged 18 or over.

When the date of a misconduct hearing is confirmed, the details will be published below. Due to the MDP being a national force the location of the misconduct hearing may vary (dependent upon the case).

Please note the following conditions of entry:

any member of the public or press wishing to attend must register in advance, by the specified closing date, and using the MDP misconduct hearing registration form ( PDF , 178 KB , 2 pages ) they must also provide valid photo identification (for example passport or driving licence) upon attendance. (To fill out the misconduct hearing form on a mobile device you must make sure that the PDF is opened in the editable mode.)

any person who is a witness at the proceedings will not be permitted to attend prior to giving their evidence but, may be permitted to take a seat in the public gallery after this time

priority will be given to interested parties and attendance will then be granted on a ‘first come, first served’ basis (up to the capacity of the venue)

any restrictions on reporting will be notified in advance of the hearing

members of the public and press are to remain silent at all times while the hearing is in session

no photographs, film or sound recording are permitted; mobile phones and other devices can be retained but must be switched off during the hearing

any conditions particular to an individual hearing will be published on this page in advance of the hearing

where a hearing is adjourned for an extended period, attendees may be expected to leave the premises and return at the appointed time; if the hearing is held within an MOD establishment members of the public and press will be escorted from the gate to the venue and back; they will not be permitted to leave the venue except to leave the establishment

no food or refreshments, with the exclusion of water, will be permitted in the hearing room; however, an area will be set aside for use by members of the public when the panel adjourn for short periods of time

no refreshments will be provided by the MDP and if held at an MOD establishment, there may be no facilities to purchase food; in this instance, attendees should be self sufficient

we cannot reimburse any expenses you incur by attending and please note that in some cases a hearing may be cancelled at short notice; in these situations, we will do our best to notify you but, it may not be possible

members of the public and press, together with any bags, will be subject to a security search as a condition of entry and exit; anything that can be used or adapted to cause injury or damage will not be permitted

If you require disabled access, or have any other reasonable adjustment requirements, please advise us of your requirements on your registration form.

Once all applications to attend have been received and reviewed (after the closing date), your attendance will be confirmed, as applicable, by the means identified on your registration form.

Please note: in exceptional circumstances, the Chair can exclude anyone from all or part of the hearing at his/her discretion and may impose conditions relating to the attendance of any person.

Should the Secretary of State for Defence consider it expedient in the interests of national security, he/she may also give direction that:

all or part of the hearing must be conducted in private

a specified person must be excluded from all or part of the hearing

specific steps are taken to conceal the identity of a witness

specific information must be excluded from the published notification of misconduct hearings or notification of outcome

If a decision is made to hold a hearing in private the reasons will be published below and, where conditions are placed on any person’s attendance, that person will be notified prior to commencement of the hearing.

Subject Officer: PC Murray

Hearing date: 30 September 2026

Alleged Conduct (& PSPBs breached):

It is alleged that on eight occasions between May and December 2024 the Officer made expense claims for £699.88 while on rest days and/or on leave. It is alleged that this was in contravention of the MOD Travel and Subsistence Policy.

It is alleged that the Officer has breached the following standards of professional behaviour:

honesty and integrity

orders and instructions

duties and responsibilities

Members of the press or public wishing to attend the Misconduct Hearing must register to do so. Anyone who has not pre-registered will not be allowed to access the hearing. Those attending are not allowed to record or film the proceedings.

Members of the media and public may attend subject to the following conditions:

the taking of photographs and the use of film or sound recording equipment during the hearing, except for official use, is prohibited

any accredited member of the media attending the hearing by the video conference link must produce valid identification if required to do so

there may be parts of the hearing which are held in private session; if that is the case, any accredited member of the media or public attending the hearing will be asked to leave during the private session, and will be informed by the Hearings Officer when they can return

To register, email MDP -PSD-GMB@mod.gov.uk with the following details:

contact telephone number

your email address

All requests to attend must be received on or before 28 September 2026

Subject Officer: PC Fergusson

Hearing date: 21 – 25 September 2026

PC Fergusson will answer allegations that she breached the Standards of Professional Behaviour set out in Schedule 3 to the Ministry of Defence Police (Conduct, Performance and Appeals Tribunals) Regulations 2020.

It is alleged that:

while on detached duty to the Ministry of Defence Police’s Professional Standards Department (PSD), PC Fergusson accessed the PSD computer system to access cases concerning other officers without having a legitimate policing purpose to do so

PC Fergusson breached the Standards of ‘Orders and Instructions’, ‘Duties and Responsibilities’, ‘Confidentiality’, and ‘Discreditable Conduct’

PC Fergusson’s conduct, if proven, amounts to gross misconduct or, in the alternative, misconduct

All requests to attend must be received on or before 14 September 2026.

Upcoming police appeals tribunals

There are currently no upcoming police tribunals.

Previous hearings and outcomes

Subject Officer: FPS Kay

Hearing date: 1 September 2026

Alleged Conduct (and PSPBs breached):

It is alleged that former PS David Kay breached the following standards of professional behaviour:

Honesty and Integrity

It is alleged that the officer breached the standards of professional behaviour by, whilst still serving in the MDP , misrepresenting that he was not a serving member of the force on LinkedIn, in order to benefit his personal electrical company.

It is alleged that this conduct, if proved, amounts to gross misconduct.

Finding : Gross Misconduct

Outcome : Dismissed without notice if still serving

Read the full outcome report: FPS Kay MDP Chair's Finding and Outcome ( PDF , 92.2 KB , 11 pages )

Previous police appeals tribunals and outcomes

items.title: UK’s Healey puts defense in focus for reindustrialization push
items.author: Alistair Smout and Elizabeth Piper, Reuters
items.summary: British government leaders are converging around the message that the defense sector will be key in energizing the nation's anemic growth.
items.body:
LIVERPOOL, England — British finance minister John Healey will put his support firmly behind firms investing in defense on Monday, part of what he will describe as a new industrialization drive to try to spur the nation’s anaemic economic growth.

In his first speech to the governing Labour Party’s annual conference as finance minister, Healey will aim to put flesh on the bones of Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s pledge to reindustrialize Britain when he became the nation’s seventh leader in a decade in July.

Healey, who resigned as defense minister under former Prime Minister Keir Starmer over what he felt was inadequate spending on defense, will say a “new age of industrialization” will see British firms deliver multi-billion pound defense projects, such as three new floating docks for submarines in Clyde in Scotland.

“By backing British shipyards, we are not only boosting national security but also securing resilience in the industries that will drive growth today while building the capabilities the country needs for the future,” Healey said in a statement.

Burnham has pledged to meet a NATO target of increasing the core defense budget to 3.5% of GDP by 2035.

Burnham eyes defense-sector jobs

The announcement is a taste of what Healey hopes to signal with his speech — that Burnham’s government hopes the route to boosting growth and reducing unemployment, and the welfare bill, will stem from new jobs created by investments in sectors such as defense.

At a conference aimed at firing up Labour members and lawmakers with a message of hope, the new government also has a difficult task in navigating competing pressures — Burnham has promised to offer the public breathing space from cost-of-living pressures, but there is a cost to that.

With conflict in the Middle East impacting energy costs and government finances tight ahead of Healey’s first budget on Oct. 28, Britain’s new finance minister has little room to maneuver.

On defense, his government also faces the need to fill a £4.7 billion ($6.2 billion) gap in its Defence Investment Plan, a blueprint some military experts say does not go far enough in meeting Britain’s promise to increase defense spending.

Healey has as yet not set out whether the government will reach defense spending of 3% of GDP by 2030 — a target he wanted but failed to persuade Starmer to sign up to, part of the reason he quit as defense minister.

Burnham’s new defense minister Wes Streeting said defense would drive Britain’s reindustrialization.

“Defense spending should make Britain stronger in every sense,” Streeting said. “That means backing British by buying British wherever our industry can deliver.”

items.title: Counterterror and Great Power Competition in the Sahel
items.author: Sean M. Zeigler
items.summary: This study develops a game-theoretic model to explain why jihadist expansion has strained traditional Western partnerships and encouraged governments to seek Russian assistance.
items.body:
ResearchPosted on rand.org Sep 28, 2026Published in: Defence and Peace Economics, Volume 37, Issue 6, pages 960-980 (2026). DOI: 10.1080/10242694.2026.2687488

The Sahel has become the epicenter of global terrorism, accounting for half of all terrorism-related fatalities by 2024. Jihadist groups pursuing system-transforming agendas have expanded across the region by aligning with local militant actors and building durable insurgencies. Their growth has disrupted longstanding security relationships between Sahelian governments and France, the United States, and the United Kingdom, with many of these new states reorienting and seeking security support from Russia. This study develops a game-theoretic model to explain why jihadist expansion has strained traditional Western partnerships and encouraged governments to seek Russian assistance. We also present an alternative model demonstrating how negotiated settlements can reduce jihadist appeal and limit external rival influence. We show that jihadist groups enhance local militants’ capabilities, reducing prospects for negotiated settlements with host states. At the same time, jihadist intervention increases the political and military costs borne by Western partners, weakening their capacity to sustain long-term security commitments. These dynamics create opportunities for Russia to expand its influence by offering security services through mercenary forces that profit from ongoing conflict. We conclude that arming host states is likely to prolong conflict, whereas negotiation and peace aid can isolate jihadist groups and promote a more stable peace.

items.title: Implementing A Public Health Approach to Preventing Violence Against Children
items.author: Ana FitzSimons
items.summary: This brief explores Brazil’s experience of implementing a public health approach to violence against children and adolescents, including the core elements as well as factors that are perceived to help and hinder implementation.
items.body:
Country Brief: Brazil

ResearchPosted on rand.org Sep 28, 2026Published in: End Violence Against Children Conference website (2026)

This brief explores Brazil’s experience of implementing a public health approach to violence against children and adolescents (VACA), including the core elements as well as factors that are perceived to help and hinder implementation. It analyses four key areas: 1) Policy & funding context; 2) Data & evidence; 3) Supporting the health sector; and 4) Multisector collaboration. The aim is to identify lessons to inform global progress in preventing VACA to 2030 and beyond. The brief draws on a desk review of relevant literature, data and legislation, as well as four interviews with key stakeholders, who were purposively sampled using the networks of the WHO and the brief’s authors.

items.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence Use and Adolescent Mental Health
items.author: Jason M. Lavender
items.summary: This paper synthesizes recent literature on the relationships between GenAI use and adolescents’ mental health, with particular attention to problematic use and psychiatric vulnerabilities.
items.body:
ResearchPosted on rand.org Sep 28, 2026Published in: Current Pediatrics Reports, Volume 14, Article Number 16 (2026). DOI: 10.1007/s40124-026-00388-8

To synthesize recent literature on the relationships between generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) use and adolescents’ mental health, with particular attention to problematic use and psychiatric vulnerabilities.

Emerging evidence suggests associations between GenAI use and a range of adolescent mental health outcomes, including depression, anxiety, psychosis-related experiences, externalizing behaviors, eating disorder risk, and suicidality. Problematic patterns of use, including dependency and emotional reliance, may be particularly relevant among adolescents with preexisting psychiatric vulnerabilities. Current evidence suggests that these relationships may be bidirectional: psychological distress can motivate GenAI use for companionship, emotional support, or escape, while problematic use may reinforce maladaptive beliefs, displace real-world relationships, and amplify existing vulnerabilities. However, evidence remains predominantly cross-sectional, limiting causal inference.

GenAI may interact with and amplify underlying psychiatric vulnerabilities during adolescence, highlighting the importance of understanding patterns and motivations of use. Pediatricians and other clinicians caring for adolescents could consider not only the frequency of GenAI use but also motivations for use, problematic dependency, and socioemotional reliance. Identifying high-risk usage patterns of GenAI through longitudinal research, particularly among youth with preexisting psychiatric risks, may inform the development of tailored screening, intervention, and prevention strategies.

items.title: From Policy to Practice
items.author: Elizabeth D. Steiner
items.summary: We investigated the role that state policies related to preschool curriculum play in public school pre-K teachers’ reported curricula use across the United States.
items.body:
How State Policies Relate to Public Pre-K Teachers’ Curriculum Use

ResearchPosted on rand.org Sep 28, 2026Published in: National Institute for Early Education Research website (2026)

As many states expand the number of pre-K seats in public schools, policymakers are focused on better understanding the role of curriculum in ensuring high-quality early childhood education environments. By combining data from the National Institute for Early Education Research’s State of Preschool Yearbook with data from RAND's American Pre-K Teacher Survey, we investigated the role that state policies related to preschool curriculum play in public school pre-K teachers’ reported curricula use across the United States. We find substantial variation in the curricula teachers report using across states, and some differences across pre-K programs within states. In addition, specific state curriculum guidance appears to influence classroom curriculum use. When states required that teachers use specific curricula (rather than recommending curricula), teachers reported combining fewer curricula in their classrooms.

items.title: Private Equity Ownership and Artificial Intelligence Adoption by Hospitals in the United States
items.author: Yashaswini Singh
items.summary: We examined the association between private equity hospital ownership and the likelihood of artificial intelligence technology adoption.
items.body:
ResearchPosted on rand.org Sep 28, 2026Published in: Health Affairs Scholar, qxag261 (2026). DOI: 10.1093/haschl/qxag261

Private equity (PE) firms own a growing share of United States hospitals and claim that capital infusions support technology investment. We examined the association between PE hospital ownership and the likelihood of artificial intelligence (AI) technology adoption.

We linked the 2024 American Hospital Association Annual Survey to a database of PE acquisitions and exits. Mixed-effects logistic models estimated any, clinical, and operational AI adoption by hospital ownership type, adjusting for hospital and market characteristics. In secondary analyses, we examined challenges to AI implementation.

PE-owned hospitals had higher adjusted adoption of any AI (difference, 24.5 percentage points; 95% confidence interval, 11.2 to 37.8) and clinical AI (difference, 27.5 percentage points; 95% confidence interval, 14.0 to 41.1) than other for-profit hospitals but did not differ from not-for-profit hospitals. Operational adoption did not differ by ownership. In secondary analyses, not-for-profit hospitals reported any, cost and resource, and regulatory and safety challenges more often than PE-owned hospitals; PE-owned hospitals reported staff-training challenges more often than other for-profit hospitals.

PE-owned and not-for-profit hospitals had similar adoption of any and clinical AI, and both exceeded other for-profit hospitals, consistent with a capital access advantage that does not extend to the broader for-profit sector.

items.title: Researchers Are Not Blank Slates
items.author: Lori Uscher-Pines
items.summary: This paper examines the implementation of a researcher self-disclosure approach where researchers shared aspects of their identity and background in interviews with Latina and Black parents participating in a clinical trial on telelactation support.
items.body: Qualitative interviews are central to social research, yet the dynamics of rapport, power, and researcher reflexivity remain complex and underexplored. This paper examines the implementation of an intentional researcher self-disclosure approach where researchers shared aspects of their identity and background in interviews with Latina and Black parents participating in a clinical trial on telelactation support. Drawing on an equity-centered model, we adapted our interview guide to foster trust and richer dialogue. Comparative analysis of interviews conducted before and after this adaptation revealed increased depth and breadth of participant responses, particularly regarding cultural, community, and family influences on breastfeeding. Our findings highlight the potential and challenges of researcher self-disclosure, offering insights for more patient-centered and effective qualitative research. We share lessons learned and offer best practices for researchers who wish to incorporate this approach in their interviewing practice.

items.title: Healey pledges “new age of industrialisation” as Government backs British shipbuilding
items.summary: Two major maritime projects to be part of “new age of industrialisation” for Britain.
items.body:
Government backs British shipyards with multi-billion pound investment in three major maritime projects to strengthen national security, support skilled jobs and drive growth in every part of the UK.

Chancellor confirms three new floating docks for the Royal Navy’s submarine service at HM Naval Base Clyde will be built in Britain supporting Britain’s defence industrial base and securing key sovereign capabilities.

New marine research vessel to be built in a British shipyard, backing coastal communities, sustainable fishing and long-term economic growth.

British shipyards will be at the heart of two major maritime projects worth billions of pounds, helping to create high-skilled jobs, drive growth and strengthen the UK’s long-term industrial and national security capabilities.

Chancellor John Healey will pledge a “new age of industrialisation” for Britain today as he confirms the multi-billion pound projects will be built by British workers, supporting jobs and a pipeline of small British businesses.

Healey will confirm that the Royal Navy’s submarine service at HM Naval Base Clyde will receive three new floating docks - known as Programme Euston - through a UK-only competition, in light of their importance to national security and sovereign British industry.

The new facilities will provide crucial maintenance for the UK’s current and future fleet of nuclear submarines, allowing essential inspections, upgrades and repairs to be carried out.

In addition to this, the Chancellor has also committed to funding for a new marine research vessel to help protect our seas. Set to be operational in the early 2030s, it will continue the delivery of core research on our seas and oceans, replacing the current vessel which is nearing the end of its life.

The evidence it collects will help ensure the security of our seas, support sustainable fishing and give coastal communities confidence that fish stocks are being managed for the future.

Both projects will be delivered by UK companies, as part of a greater focus on how government spends taxpayers’ money to boost national security whilst also supporting British jobs and growth in local communities.

Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey said:

“Britain has a proud shipbuilding heritage, and every pound of this strategic investment in a critical sector is backing British jobs on the Clyde and businesses across the UK, supporting growth in every postcode.

“By backing British shipyards, we are not only boosting national security but also securing resilience in the industries that will drive growth today while building the capabilities the country needs for the future.”

Defence Secretary, Wes Streeting said:

“Defence spending should make Britain stronger in every sense. That means backing British by buying British wherever our industry can deliver.

“HM Naval Base Clyde is at the heart of our submarine service. Programme Euston will modernise it for decades to come, while backing British shipyards, workers and engineering.

“That is defence driving the reindustrialisation of Britain and strengthening our sovereign capability.”

items.title: UK Thwarts Suspected Terrorist Plot Against Base Used by US Bombers for Strikes on Iran
items.author: Chris Gordon
items.summary: An air base in England used by American bombers to strike Iran was the target of a suspected bomb plot, U.K. officials said Sept. 27. The post UK Thwarts Suspected Terrorist Plot Against Base Used by US Bombers for Strikes on Iran appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
An air base in England where American bombers used to strike Iran are based was the target of a suspected bomb plot, U.K. officials said Sept. 27.

Five men were arrested on suspicion of terrorism and explosives offenses after being stopped close to RAF Fairford, police said, and explosive ordnance disposal technicians were dispatched to the scene. RAF Fairford is a British base currently hosting a dozen B-1B Lancer bombers, which have been stationed there for around seven months for strikes on Iran.

President Donald Trump said the suspects were “looking to do big damage” to the U.S. at RAF Fairford and called the arrests “fantastic” before boarding Air Force One on Sept. 27.

“We had them under view for a long time and we got them,” Trump added. “Working with Britain, it was an amazing job. We had them under investigation.”

The base has been under increased security for days, which included the placement of vehicles around the perimeter, people familiar with the matter said. The threat level at the base was raised before the suspects were arrested. A U.S. Air Force spokesperson declined to discuss specific force protection measures, citing operational security.

Explosive ordnance teams from the British Army were called in to inspect the scene, and helicopter video footage aired by multiple U.K. news outlets showed a robot and personnel inspecting three white vans near the base fence, with B-1Bs parked on base nearby.

“The safety and security of the public is our first priority, and I want people to know that we will always take every step necessary to protect our communities and keep our country safe,” British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said in a statement.

Police said they were called by a local after receiving a report about three suspicious vehicles near RAF Fairford, which is located in Gloucestershire in southwest England.

“At around 12:45 a.m. today … police received a call relating to three suspicious vehicles which appeared to be traveling towards the air base,” the Metropolitan Police, which investigates terrorism cases in the U.K., said in a Sept. 27 statement.

The U.K. government is still investigating the incident, counterterrorism officials said.

“We are in the early stages of an investigation, and five men remain in custody,” counterterrorism policing senior national coordinator Vicki Evans said. “As you would expect, we are working closely with our partners to understand the circumstances of the incident.”

RAF Fairford does not have permanent U.S. Air Force aircraft assigned there, but it has a wing dedicated to supporting U.S. operations and is considered the main U.S. bomber site in Europe, having regularly hosted U.S. aircraft for years.

“The 501st Combat Support Wing and our other U.K.-based wings remain vigilant and will take appropriate actions to ensure the safety and security of our U.S. service members, civilians, contractors, and their families,” the Air Force spokesperson said. “We constantly assess a variety of factors that determine what measures we institute or modify to protect our installations, our people, and their families.”

Roadblocks, large machinery, and armed police have been seen around the base. Eighty-five homes in the nearby village of Whelford were evacuated.

“The emergency services have well-rehearsed plans for dealing with major incidents,” Gloucestershire Police assistant chief constable Richard Ocone said. “A cordon is in place as a precaution and the public can expect to see an emergency services presence in the area for some time.”

The B-1Bs at Fairford were heavily used during Operation Epic Fury, the large-scale air campaign against Iran in the spring, when the base housed some two dozen bombers including B-52 Stratofortresses.

Since a shaky ceasefire in April, most of the B-1Bs have remained while the U.S. carried out occasional strikes, including at least one involving a B-1 from Fairford. The bombers have regularly conducted training sorties out of the U.K.

The U.K. government gave permission for the base to be used in strikes on Iran in March under former Prime Minister Kier Starmer, for what the U.K. considers collective self-defense strikes. Burnham reaffirmed that decision in July, and Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps warned the U.K. government that it considered Fairford a legitimate target for attack. The U.K. government said in July it was prepared to use the British armed forces to defend the base.

The U.S. Air Force said it would continue to cooperate with the U.K. government to ensure the safety of its bases in Britain. Another U.K. base with U.S. aircraft is RAF Lakenheath, which hosts F-35A Lightning II and F-15E Strike Eagle fighters that have deployed to the Middle East for operations against Iran. Lakenheath is also used as a stopover location for fighters heading to the Middle East from the U.S.

“The safety and security of our Airmen, families, and surrounding communities remains our highest priority,” the Air Force spokesperson said. “We remain in close coordination with our U.K. partners to help ensure the safety and security of both our military and local communities.”

items.title: Terror suspects wanted to do ‘big damage’ to air base used by US, Trump says
items.author: Toby Shepheard, Reuters
items.summary: British police on Sunday arrested five men on suspicion of explosive and terrorism offenses near an air base that hosts U.S. Air Force personnel.
items.body:
British police on Sunday arrested five men near an air base used by U.S. forces on suspicion of explosive and terrorism offenses after a tip that three vans were heading to the military airfield, which has been used to strike Iran.

U.S. President Donald Trump said the suspects had been looking to do “big damage” and had been under investigation by British and U.S. authorities.

British counter terrorism detectives leading the investigation said police received a call about three suspicious vehicles that appeared to be traveling towards RAF Fairford in the west of England in the early hours of Sunday.

Five men were arrested by armed officers and later held on suspicion of preparation of a terrorist act. Police said they believed the incident was now contained.

POLICE WORKING TO UNDERSTAND CIRCUMSTANCES

“We are in the early stages of an investigation, and five men remain in custody,” Counter Terrorism Policing Senior National Coordinator Vicki Evans said in a statement.

“As you would expect, we are working closely with our partners to understand the circumstances of the incident.”

Police said a 400-meter cordon was in place around the base as the bomb disposal unit investigated the vans. Local residents in 85 homes in a nearby village were evacuated, and armed officers were patrolling the site.

The British government, which has given authorization to the U.S. to use bombers based at Fairford to strike Iranian missile sites that were attacking ships in the Strait of Hormuz, said Prime Minister Andy Burnham was being updated on the incident.

“I know today’s incident near RAF Fairford will be deeply concerning for local residents and for many people following developments across the country,” Burnham wrote on X.

Britain said in July its armed forces were ready to protect the country from any attack after Iran’s Revolutionary Guards warned it not to allow U.S. bombers to fly from Fairford, saying any base used to launch attacks would be a legitimate target.

Police have not said who they believed was involved in Sunday’s alleged incident. An Iranian-linked motive is considered the most likely, a source familiar with the investigation said, while a Russian sabotage operation or an Islamist plot are also being looked at.

“The arrest in the UK was fantastic,” Trump told reporters, saying it was “an amazing job.”

“We had them under investigation. They were looking to do big damage to our port and working with the British worked out great. ... We had them under view for a long time, and we got them,” Trump added.

On Sunday morning the base was blocked by armed police while large machinery also prevented access. Reuters witnesses said security had been increased at other bases used by the U.S., with armored vehicles and soldiers at the gates of RAF Lakenheath and RAF Mildenhall in eastern England.

DECLARATION OF A MAJOR INCIDENT

“A cordon is in place as a precaution, and the public can expect to see an emergency services presence in the area for some time,” Gloucestershire Police Assistant Chief Constable Richard Ocone told reporters.

The Daily Mail website carried a photograph of five men without shirts who it said had been arrested.

A spokesperson for the U.S. Air Force declined to discuss specific force protection measures.

“The 501st Combat Support Wing and our fellow UK-based Wings remain vigilant and will take appropriate actions to ensure the safety and security of our U.S. service members, civilians, contractors, and their families,” the spokesperson said.

“We constantly assess a variety of factors that determine what measures we institute or modify to protect our installations, our people and their families.”

British ministers have also previously briefed providers of critical infrastructure on the threat posed by Russia, with the government increasingly concerned about possible sabotage operations and cyberattacks.

Russia denies mounting hybrid attacks on Western nations.

A British military air base in central England was broken into in June 2025 by the Palestine Action protest group, which has since been proscribed as a terrorist organization.

items.title: To Secure Arctic, NORTHCOM Builds Closer Ties to Pacific, European Commands
items.author: Chris Gordon
items.summary: U.S. Northern Command plans to sign an agreement with its European and Pacific counterparts to enhance coordination and close security seams in the Arctic, a strategically vital region that spans all three commands. The agreement comes at an important moment in NORTHCOM's evolution, as its mission grows more complex. The post To Secure Arctic, NORTHCOM Builds Closer Ties to Pacific, European Commands appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine</a
items.body:
U.S. Northern Command plans to sign an agreement with its European and Pacific counterparts to enhance coordination and close security seams in the Arctic, a strategically vital region where all three commands converge, U.S. officials told Air & Space Forces Magazine.

NORTHCOM’s Gen. Gregory M. Guillot, U.S. European Command’s Gen. Alexus G. Grynkewich, and U.S. Pacific Command’s Adm. Samuel Paparo will finalize the agreement, which aims to strengthen information sharing and ensure that adversaries cannot exploit the geographic boundaries among the commands.

U.S. Northern Command’s long-standing motto, “We have the watch,” has taken on greater urgency in recent years as the potential means to attack the U.S. Arctic region have grown. Today, the command’s geographic focus stretches across Canada, Greenland, and south to Mexico and parts of the Caribbean, and the potential dangers have expanded to include a range of emerging threats, from intelligence-gathering balloons to ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, and drones.

Guillot, in a September interview with Air & Space Forces Magazine, said the command has managed the growth well. “Over the last couple of years, we’ve received a few new missions with Greenland, the Southern Border, Golden Dome, and the counter-UAS mission, and we’ve been able to evolve and incorporate those into our daily homeland defense operations, I think, seamlessly,” said Guillot, whose responsibilities also include heading the binational U.S.-Canadian North American Aerospace Defense Command, known as NORAD.

“The command is growing as the number of threats and the number of avenues of approach that they can use to threaten us increase,” he added of NORTHCOM.

The Arctic’s strategic importance has grown as melting polar ice has opened up the region for greater commercial traffic and resource exploitation.

Russia, which owns more than half the Arctic coastline, has long projected its military might in the region.

More recently, China has sought to assert itself as an Arctic nation, not because it controls territory there but because of its value as a transit venue, shortening the trade routes between China and Europe. China operates research vessels there, including submersibles.

“They’re seeking to move themselves forward militarily and become global power projectors, not regional power projectors, and part of that will involve holding us at risk through the Arctic and ensuring that policy in the Arctic reflects their interests,” retired Gen. Glen D. VanHerck, Guillot’s predecessor at NORTHCOM and NORAD, said in an interview.

A joint China-Russia bomber patrol in the region, which took off in 2024 from a Russian base, demonstrated closer ties between the two and raised concerns across North America and Europe about their growing cooperation.

“When you see Russia and China cooperating militarily in the Arctic, with a greater capacity arguably than anywhere else on Earth, I think that should give some signals that we should be paying attention to what’s going on in the region,” said Iris Ferguson, who served as deputy assistant secretary of defense for Arctic and global resilience from 2022-2025.

Ferguson sees closing the gaps between U.S. military commands that converge in the Arctic region as essential to enhanced security.

“There are multiple seams in the Arctic for the United States,” she said. “The one between NORTHCOM and EUCOM is a significant one and is one area that deserves more attention.”

NORTHCOM led the drive to formalize an agreement with its fellow combatant commands, working closely with EUCOM and its boss, Grynkewich, who is also NATO’s Supreme Allied Commander Europe, with critical ties to NATO’s Nordic allies. Through NATO, Grynkewich is responsible for defending what NATO dubs the High North, comprising Canada, Finland, Norway, Sweden, Denmark, Iceland, and the U.S. The alliance held multiple large-scale Arctic exercises this past summer, some of which Air & Space Forces Magazine experienced firsthand. NATO’s Arctic Sentry “enhanced vigilance activity” operates in cooperation with NORAD and NORTHCOM, and alliance officials describe that cooperation as at a level not seen in decades.

Guillot said the potential threats aren’t limited to America’s largest potential adversaries.

“I see the threat to our continent changing not just from Russia and China, but from multiple adversaries,” Guillot said. “The biggest change is that it’s from all avenues of approach instead of just from the north, and it’s with systems that could affect us from further away. So therefore our defense capabilities need to be expanded further from our borders to make sure that we’re defending at the appropriate range.”

“What that necessitates is cooperation with EUCOM, PACOM, and SOUTHCOM, where we can exchange information, pictures, intelligence, and even resources to defend further away,” Guillot said.

VanHerck applauded efforts to strengthen Arctic security and stop threats before they reach North America.

“Homeland defense doesn’t start in the homeland,” VanHerck said. “It starts forward with allies and partners and fellow combat commanders forward. Ideally, you have a posture and a presence and enough domain awareness that you deter those activities before they ever start. And if they’re going to attack, you can defeat those adversaries or capabilities further forward.”

The Trump administration has made Arctic security a centerpiece of its foreign policy, pressing to win new concessions for American basing in Greenland, expanding beyond a single Space Force installation to establish two new bases. Demonstrating the critical nature of Greenland to North American security, the administration transferred responsibility for Greenland, a territory of Denmark, to U.S. Northern Command, removing it from U.S. European Command’s area of responsibility.

That transfer is far from symbolic. “A lot of exercises and operations that we would normally conduct either unilaterally, or perhaps with Canada through NORAD, we’re now doing with other countries to include Denmark,” Guillot said.

A recent exercise with the U.S. and allied nations marked the first time Danish F-35s landed in Greenland.

U.S., Canadian, and Danish forces conducted joint Operation Arctic Vanguard and NATO exercises in Greenland this month that drew F-35As from continental U.S. bases, U.S. F-16s from Alaska, Canadian CF-18s, and Danish F-35As. French air-to-air refueling aircraft and NATO-operated E-3 AWACS command-and-control jets also joined the operations as part of NATO’s Arctic Sentry.

Referencing the recent exercises, Guillot said allies were “fully integrated” and “operating in multiple lanes at the same time,” a shift from a few years ago when the U.S. may have conducted unilateral training instead. Operating as an integrated whole creates dilemmas for adversaries and acts as a force multiplier for the allies.

“That is possible due to the great relationship and partnering by the Danish forces,” Guillot said.

On the other side of North America, near Alaska, the U.S. and Canada recently conducted a joint exercise practicing striking maritime targets in the Bering Sea, using aircraft, surface vessels, and a submarine. The U.S. has also conducted joint naval operations with Canada that involve the U.S. Coast Guard alongside the U.S. military. Those exercises fall under Operation Tundra Merlin, which focuses on deterrence near Alaska, including the western Arctic and Northern Pacific. Pacific Air Forces aircraft stationed in Alaska also supported Arctic Vanguard on the other side of NORTHCOM’s region.

Alaska’s geographic size and placement at the nexus of the NORTHCOM and PACOM areas of responsibility places it in proximity to potential threats from China, Russia, and North Korea.

“I don’t think people appreciate the role that Alaska plays for our homeland defense mission, but also for our Indo-Pacific mission,” said Ferguson, who also served as a senior advisor to the Air Force on the Arctic. “Alaska is critical as a place of power projection to be able to project power not only into the Indo-Pacific in the event of a contingency, but also into the European theater.”

The exercises underscore Guillot’s broader Nordic Bridge initiative, launched earlier this year to better integrate allied operations across the Arctic. It includes coordination among the various U.S. combatant commands that touch on the region, as well as Canada, Sweden, Finland, Denmark, Norway, and Iceland, all NATO allies. Working together, they aim to enhance domain awareness and interoperability.

“We’re working with other friendly Arctic nations to increase our presence,” Guillot said, “to increase and expand the deterrence, and make sure that every exercise we do up there is multinational and along multiple avenues of approach.”

items.title: Air Force Certifies Anduril Barracuda Cruise Missile for Open System Updates
items.author: Todd South
items.summary: The Anduril-built Barracuda cruise missile recently received certification as the Air Force’s first large-scale production munition compliant with open systems architecture. The post Air Force Certifies Anduril Barracuda Cruise Missile for Open System Updates appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
The Anduril-built Barracuda cruise missile recently received certification as the Air Force’s first large-scale production munition compliant with open systems architecture.

The certification clears the way for the new weapon, billed as a way for commanders to carry multiple tools in their belts, with options to swap payloads and other features once the missile is delivered to the Air Force.

“Barracuda’s open software architecture means that it can be equipped with a variety of different datalinks and communications modalities, unlocking integrations with a vast spectrum of different aircraft and other communications nodes,” an Anduril spokesperson told Air & Space Forces Magazine Sept. 25.

Anduril is slated to deliver its first Barracuda missiles to the Pentagon in early 2027.

The Air Force Research Laboratory’s Munition Open Architecture Test and Evaluation Laboratory, or MOATEL, oversees the Weapon Open System Architecture certification process. The lab’s engineers spent four days at Anduril’s California headquarters verifying compliance with open system architecture, known as WOSA, on Anduril hardware, an Anduril spokesperson said.

“This is showing that open architecture can scale beyond prototypes,” Jonathan Shaver, program manager and creator of WOSA at AFRL’s Air Warfare Directorate, said in an Anduril release. “Without that independent path from S&T to MOATEL, the industrial base cannot deliver new technology to the warfighter at the speed the fight requires.”

The certified modularity option for the cruise missile could give commanders a plethora of features to work with in the planned-for stockpile boost.

The Pentagon announced multi-year framework agreements for its Family of Affordable Mass Missiles program in July. Anduril, CoAspire, and Zone 5 Technologies were selected. The agreements call for the three companies to produce 8,000 missiles annually once production ramps up. That timeline targets 5,300 missiles in 2028, rising to 8,000 by 2031.

The MOATEL verification tested 14 WOSA domains: Mission Autonomy, Seeker, Inertial Measurement Unit, GPS, Air-Data Sensor, Propulsion, Airframe Control, Target State Estimator, Altimeter Aiding Navigation, Clock, Autopilot, Guidance, Navigation, and Munitions Data Bus.

“It’s easy to talk about modularity and open architectures in the abstract. Proving it through an independent assessment is harder,” Pat Morris, vice president of advanced effects at Anduril, said in the release.

With the MOATEL assessment, those munitions can be updated and upgraded as users need new technology or as mission requirements change.

Modular Munitions Options

Anduril has integrated four different turbojet engines into the Barracuda 500, giving the company flexibility in providing engines as it seeks to churn out missiles in the coming years.

The MOATEL assessment’s certification of the open-architecture software also clears the way to use the Barracuda with current and future communication systems.

So far, the company has built three base model Barracudas: the Barracuda 100, with a roughly 35-pound payload and a range of more than 120 nautical miles; the Barracuda 250, also with a 35-pound payload and a range of more than 200 nautical miles; and the Barracuda 500, with a greater than 100-pound payload and more than 500 nautical miles of range. The company spokesperson said the WOSA verification applies across the Barracuda variants.

During AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference last week, Lockheed Martin announced its new AGM-158 FLEX. The munitions provide modularity, including swappable nose and launch options for the precision-guided Joint Air-to-Surface Standoff Missile, known as the JASSM, and its companion Long-Range Anti-Ship Missile, or LRASM.

The Air Force Life Cycle Management Center at Eglin Air Force Base, Florida, posted a notice to industry seeking modular parts for its Extended Range Attack Munition in January 2025, signaling a push toward broader munitions options for the stockpile that the service and other branches are now building.
items.titleZh: 美空军认证Anduril“梭鱼”巡航导弹可进行开放系统升级
items.summaryZh: 由Anduril公司制造的“梭鱼”巡航导弹近日获得认证，成为美国空军首款符合开放系统架构的大规模生产弹药。
items.zhFull:
由Anduril公司制造的Barracuda巡航导弹近日获得认证，成为美国空军首款符合开放系统架构的大规模生产弹药。

该认证为这款新武器扫清了道路。它被宣传为一种让指挥官“腰带上多揣几件工具”的手段——导弹交付空军后，还可选择更换有效载荷及其他功能配置。

Anduril公司发言人9月25日对《空军与太空军杂志》表示：“Barracuda的开放软件架构意味着它可以配备多种不同的数据链和通信方式，从而能够与种类繁多的各类飞机及其他通信节点实现集成。”

Anduril公司计划于2027年初向五角大楼交付首批Barracuda导弹。

美国空军研究实验室下属的弹药开放架构测试与评估实验室（MOATEL）负责监督武器开放系统架构的认证流程。Anduril公司发言人称，该实验室的工程师在Anduril位于加利福尼亚州的总部驻留四天，对Anduril硬件进行了核查，确认其符合被称为WOSA的开放系统架构要求。

美国空军研究实验室空战局WOSA项目经理兼创建者乔纳森·谢弗（Jonathan Shaver）在Anduril发布的一则消息中表示：“这表明开放架构能够超越原型阶段实现规模化。如果没有从科技部门到MOATEL的这条独立路径，工业基础就无法以作战所需的速度向作战人员交付新技术。”

在计划中的库存扩充中，这款巡航导弹获得认证的模块化选项可为指挥官提供众多可供使用的功能。

五角大楼于7月宣布了其“经济型大规模导弹系列”（Family of Affordable Mass Missiles）计划的多年框架协议。Anduril、CoAspire和Zone 5 Technologies三家公司入选。协议要求这三家公司在产能提升后每年生产8000枚导弹。该时间表的目标是2028年达到5300枚，到2031年增至8000枚。

MOATEL 验证测试了 14 个 WOSA 域：任务自主、导引头、惯性测量单元、GPS、大气数据传感器、推进、机体控制、目标状态估计器、高度表辅助导航、时钟、自动驾驶仪、制导、导航和弹药数据总线。

“抽象地谈论模块化和开放架构很容易。通过独立评估来证明它则更难，”安杜里尔公司先进效应副总裁帕特·莫里斯（Pat Morris）在新闻稿中表示。

借助 MOATEL 评估，这些弹药可以在用户需要新技术或任务要求变化时进行更新和升级。

模块化弹药选项

安杜里尔已将四种不同的涡喷发动机集成到 Barracuda 500 中，这使该公司在寻求未来几年大量生产导弹时，在发动机供应方面拥有灵活性。

MOATEL 评估对开放架构软件的认证，也为将 Barracuda 与当前及未来的通信系统配合使用扫清了道路。

截至目前，该公司已制造了三种基础型号的 Barracuda：Barracuda 100，有效载荷约 35-pound，射程超过 120 nautical miles；Barracuda 250，同样具有 35-pound 的有效载荷，射程超过 200 nautical miles；以及 Barracuda 500，有效载荷超过 100-pound，射程超过 500 nautical miles。公司发言人表示，WOSA 验证适用于所有 Barracuda 变体。

上周，在 AFA 的 Air, Space & Cyber 会议上，洛克希德·马丁公司宣布了其新型 AGM-158 FLEX。这些弹药具备模块化特性，包括可为精确制导的联合空面防区外导弹（JASSM）及其配套的远程反舰导弹（LRASM）提供可更换的头部和发射选项。

佛罗里达州埃格林空军基地的美国空军寿命周期管理中心于2025年1月向工业界发布通告，为其增程攻击弹药寻求模块化部件，表明空军正推动为空军及其他军种目前正在建立的库存提供更广泛的弹药选项。

items.title: Air Force Injects $87M into IVEWS F-16 Electronic Warfare Upgrades
items.author: Todd South
items.summary: The Air Force has invested $87.4 million to upgrade the F-16 Fighting Falcon's electronic warfare capabilities, bolstering the fighter's self-protection against increasingly advanced threats. Bringing the total program value to $1.92 billion, the move is expected to jump-start fielding by funding low-rate initial production of the AN/ALQ-257 Integrated Viper Electronic Warfare Suite, or IVEWS. The post Air Force Injects $87M into IVEWS F-16 Electronic Warfare Upgrades appeared first on <
items.body:
The Air Force has invested $87.4 million to upgrade the F-16 Fighting Falcon‘s electronic warfare capabilities, bolstering the fighter’s self-protection against increasingly advanced threats.

Bringing the total program value to $1.92 billion, the move is expected to jump-start fielding by funding low-rate initial production of the AN/ALQ-257 Integrated Viper Electronic Warfare Suite, or IVEWS, which is integrated into the fighter’s airframe.

This money is intended to produce an upgraded Viper for use in the Middle East, as part of an effort pushed by the U.S. military’s Central Command.

Work on the low-rate initial production batch at the company’s Illinois facility is expected to conclude by the end of 2029. The Air Force Lifecycle Management Center, Wright-Patterson, Ohio, oversees the contract.

The company says the new EW system is sorely needed for the F-16’s future fights.

“You cannot defeat what you cannot see,” said Shalini Gupta, vice president of electronic warfare and targeting at Northrop Grumman, in a statement to Air & Space Forces Magazine. “A modern EW suite is essential for operations in contested airspace. We are producing fully functional, flight-proven systems now. From day one, our customers gain the ability to geolocate threats with a single aircraft, and the confidence that comes with having a U.S. program of record system on board.”

The F-16 has seen a lot of action in Operation Epic Fury, and while its existing capabilities have handled Iranian air defenses and electronic warfare capabilities, peer adversaries such as the Chinese military have more sophisticated means to foil the jet fighter’s aims.

The Air Force issued an urgent operational need statement in 2025 that triggered a congressionally supplied $187 million in its fiscal 2026 reconciliation bill, which sped up system qualification and flight testing.

After CENTCOM’s operational need statement, Northrop and the Air Force made the effort a priority.

“This is one of many efforts to keep our fourth-gen platforms competitive as the adversary advances,” Lt. Gen. Derek France, then-commander of Air Forces Central, said in September 2025 about IVEWS. “That’s the bumper sticker, if you will.”

The recently announced additional $87.4 million LRIP modification fuels the initial production of the Viper suites. Full-rate production of the suites for the full 450-aircraft fleet is scheduled to follow this initial batch.

The initial production tranche for the Air Force was to outfit 72 Block 50 F-16s with IVEWS, with more likely to arrive as production ramps up, the company’s vice president of targeting and survivability Jim Conroy told Air & Space Forces Magazine in a 2025 interview.

Iran operates radar-guided and electro-optical/infrared (EO/IR) air defense systems. Non-traditional Houthi air defense systems proved a particular challenge for U.S. aircraft, including F-16s, during last year’s Operation Rough Rider against the group in Yemen.

During Operation Epic Fury, the Air Force used its Block 50 F-16s in a suppression of enemy air defenses role and deployed most of its Wild Weasel SEAD F-16 units to support operations against Iran. Those units’ F-16s can carry AGM-88 anti-radiation missiles and are equipped with HARM Targeting System, or HTS, pods—a capability the Air Force’s other fourth-generation fighter, the F-15E Strike Eagle, lacks.

IVEWS is an ultra-wideband, sophisticated EW system capable of radar warning, active jamming, and detecting, identifying, and locating threats, suited for fifth- and sixth-generation aircraft.

It can also conduct single-aircraft autonomous geolocation, meaning one aircraft can find an enemy radar and map a threat while actively using the aircraft’s jammer. Older systems required multiple aircraft to triangulate a radar location and required pilots to shut off jammers when mapping threats.

Under the USAF “Big Iron” software compliance standard, teams will be able to quickly update IVEWS system software files without hardware modifications or grounding the aircraft for days, weeks, or months.

IVEWS began flight tests in 2024 and has undergone more than 550 hours of effective testing across 300 sorties during operational assessments, Northrop Vice President for Mission Systems Mike Minahan said in a July call with reporters.

The system works in conjunction with the AN/AG-83 Scalable Agile Beam Radar. The radar uses an Active Electronically Scanned Array (AESA) to enable faster target tracking.

As of mid-May, Northrop had delivered 1,000 SABR radars to its F-16 customers. The new radar uses digital tracking as opposed to the legacy AN/APG-66 and AN-APG-68 radars that it is replacing.

IVEWS, the SABR, and the upgraded LITENING LA pod, which gives the aircraft a 50 percent increase in the range of its targeting system, are crucial to keeping the aging F-16 combat-worthy. The pod is also used on the F-15E Strike Eagle, A-10 Thunderbolt II, B-52 Stratofortress, and the Navy F/A-18 Super Hornet.

IVEWS would likely be equipped on possible future Air Force new-build “F-16G” purchases the service will consider, Air & Space Forces Magazine reported.

The LITENING LA, an upgrade from the current LITENING pod, entered flight testing in December, according to Northrop officials.

items.title: Ukraine’s deadly AI training platform for drone tech opens to UK companies
items.author: Katie Livingstone
items.summary: Ukraine opens wartime battlefield data to Britain through Avengers AI Labs, giving British companies access to data for AI drone development.
items.body:
KYIV, Ukraine — The British Ministry of Defence has struck a partnership with Ukraine’s Avengers AI Labs, an information-rich platform built to train AI for battlefield drones, marking the first time that Kyiv has opened up its trove of wartime data to an outside government, according to officials in London.

The announcement comes a month after U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham signed an AI deal with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy while visiting Kyiv alongside other allies to honor Ukraine’s independence day and pledge continued support to the war-torn nation.

“Ukraine is the frontline of freedom for us all. On my recent visit to Kyiv, I saw first-hand the courage and resilience of the Ukrainian people,” U.K. Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said in a statement on Friday.

“I also saw the extraordinary innovation which is allowing them to repel Putin’s illegal and unprovoked invasion.”

“This world-first access to real battlefield data will allow British companies to continue pushing the frontier of defence innovation, deterring our enemies and making us safer at home as well as further strengthening Ukraine,” Streeting said.

Ukraine has shared its combat-derived AI training data with allies in the past, but this is the first time that Kyiv has granted a foreign country access to the machine-learning infrastructure driving its rapid AI innovations seen across the front.

Avengers AI Labs holds an annotated dataset of more than 5 million battlefield frames, plus sensor data covering millions of object detections — including tanks, artillery, air defense, infantry, Shahed drones, reconnaissance UAVs, and more) — built mainly from Ukraine’s DELTA battle-management system, according to a release by Ukrainian officials.

Data is anonymized and released on a delay to avoid endangering personnel still fighting, according to Ukraine’s Defence Ministry. U.K. companies also work inside a secure perimeter that doesn’t allow them to download the underlying dataset, according to Ukraine’s MOD.

The British defense ministry is now inviting up to a dozen companies to submit proposals for how they would use the platform, especially to develop tech that would enable full functionality even when communications are degraded or satellite navigation is unavailable.

“It is exactly the kind of practical partnership the Taskforce was set up to drive, supporting our ally Ukraine while strengthening sovereign capability here in Britain,” U.K. AI Minister Kanishka Narayan said in Friday’s statement.

Katie Livingstone is the Ukraine correspondent for Defense News and Military Times. Based in Kyiv, she has covered Russia's full-scale invasion since its first days. She is a former Fulbright fellow whose award-winning work has appeared in outlets across Europe and the U.S.
items.titleZh: 乌克兰用于无人机技术的致命AI训练平台向英国公司开放
items.summaryZh: 乌克兰通过Avengers AI Labs向英国开放战时战场数据，使英国公司能够获取数据用于AI无人机研发。
items.zhFull:
基辅，乌克兰——据伦敦官员称，英国国防部已与乌克兰的 Avengers AI Labs 建立合作关系，该实验室是一个信息丰富的平台，旨在为战场无人机训练人工智能，这标志着基辅首次向外国政府开放其战时数据宝库。

这一消息宣布的一个月前，英国首相安迪·伯纳姆（Andy Burnham）在访问基辅期间与乌克兰总统弗拉基米尔·泽连斯基（Volodymyr Zelenskyy）签署了一项人工智能协议，当时他与其他盟友一道前往基辅，纪念乌克兰独立日，并承诺继续支持这个饱受战争蹂躏的国家。

英国国防大臣韦斯·斯特里廷（Wes Streeting）在周五的一份声明中说：“乌克兰是我们所有人自由的前线。在我最近访问基辅期间，我亲眼目睹了乌克兰人民的勇气与坚韧。”

“我还看到了非凡的创新，正是这些创新让他们得以击退普京非法且无端的入侵。”

斯特里廷说：“这种全球首次获得的真实战场数据访问权限，将使英国公司能够继续推进国防创新的前沿，威慑我们的敌人，让我们在国内更安全，同时也进一步加强乌克兰。”

乌克兰过去曾与盟友分享其源自实战的人工智能训练数据，但这是基辅首次向外国开放其机器学习基础设施的访问权限，而正是这一基础设施推动着前线各地所见的人工智能快速创新。

据乌克兰官员发布的消息，Avengers AI Labs 拥有一个标注数据集，包含超过 500 万个战场帧，以及涵盖数百万次目标检测的传感器数据——包括坦克、火炮、防空系统、步兵、Shahed 无人机、侦察无人机等——主要构建自乌克兰的 DELTA 战场管理系统。

据乌克兰国防部称，数据经过匿名化处理并延迟发布，以避免危及仍在作战的人员。乌克兰国防部还表示，英国公司也在一个安全边界内工作，不允许下载底层数据集。

英国国防部目前正邀请至多12家公司提交方案，说明它们将如何使用该平台，尤其是开发相关技术，使平台即便在通信降级或卫星导航不可用时也能保持完整功能。

英国人工智能大臣卡尼什卡·纳拉扬（Kanishka Narayan）在周五的声明中表示：“这正该工作组旨在推动的那种务实伙伴关系，既支持我们的盟友乌克兰，又增强英国本土的主权能力。”

凯蒂·利文斯通（Katie Livingstone）是《防务新闻》和《军事时报》的乌克兰通讯员。她常驻基辅，自俄罗斯全面入侵最初几天起便持续进行报道。她曾是富布赖特学者，其获奖作品曾在欧洲和美国的多家媒体发表。

据乌克兰国防部称，数据经过匿名化处理并延迟发布，以避免危及仍在作战的人员。乌克兰国防部还表示，英国公司也在一个安全边界内工作，不允许下载底层数据集。
英国国防部目前正邀请至多12家公司提交方案，说明它们将如何使用该平台，尤其是开发相关技术，使平台即便在通信降级或卫星导航不可用时也能保持完整功能。
英国人工智能大臣卡尼什卡·纳拉扬（Kanishka Narayan）在周五的声明中表示：“这正该工作组旨在推动的那种务实伙伴关系，既支持我们的盟友乌克兰，又增强英国本土的主权能力。”
凯蒂·利文斯通（Katie Livingstone）是《防务新闻》和《军事时报》的乌克兰通讯员。她常驻基辅，自俄罗斯全面入侵最初几天起便持续进行报道。她曾是富布赖特学者，其获奖作品曾在欧洲和美国的多家媒体发表。

items.title: Trump administration obligates $307M for military aid to Ukraine
items.author: Patricia Zengerle and Mike Stone, Reuters
items.summary: The Trump administration has made legally binding commitments to spend almost all of the $400 million Congress approved for military aid to Ukraine.
items.body:
The Trump administration has made legally binding commitments to spend almost all of the $400 million Congress approved for military aid to Ukraine late last year, ensuring that the money will not expire on Sept. 30, according to three sources familiar with the plan.

As of early this week, $307 million of the $400 million of the Ukraine Security Assistance Initiative (USAI) funding had been obligated, said the sources, who spoke on condition of anonymity, and the administration plans to lock in the remaining $93 million before the fiscal year ends on Sept. 30.

The Pentagon, which oversees the USAI program, declined to comment for this story.

First deliveries include weapons, spare parts

The money has been a source of contention with Congress, as Democrats and some of President Donald Trump’s fellow Republicans have criticized the Pentagon for sitting on the aid for Kyiv, which members of both parties voted for last December.

Trump has in recent months taken a more positive tone toward Ukraine, signing off on a proposal to give a license for Ukraine to manufacture Patriot interceptor missiles and signing a Russia sanctions bill.

He met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy this week at UN headquarters in New York, after which Zelenskiy said they had discussed efforts to end the war with Russia, including a potential bilateral ceasefire on energy-related targets.

The first deliveries, which will include offensive weapons and equipment such as spare parts for armored vehicles, began this month. The rest are expected to be delivered before October 2029, the sources said. Trump’s White House term ends in January of that year.

The remaining $93 million in the package approved by Congress does not have to be spent by the end of the year, but it will expire if it is not formally placed under contract by then.

Patriot missiles not included

One of the sources said the military equipment did not include Patriot missiles, despite Russia bombarding Ukraine’s cities with drones and ballistic missiles.

The U.S. war in Iran and the Ukraine war have depleted global supplies of Patriots, and Kyiv has been pleading for more.

Reuters reported in July that the administration had told Congress it could take years for the equipment to reach Ukrainian forces. The Pentagon has held up shipments of weapons to Ukraine several times out of concern that US weapons supplies were too low.

Lawmakers said then they were unhappy with the Pentagon’s timeline, considered unusually slow for an ongoing conflict, and the issue has come up repeatedly at congressional hearings.

Ukraine has been by far the top recipient of U.S. foreign aid since Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, but the U.S. commitment to Kyiv has been called into question since Trump took office and his Republicans took control of both houses of Congress in January 2025.
items.titleZh: 特朗普政府拨定3.07亿美元对乌军事援助
items.summaryZh: 特朗普政府已作出具有法律约束力的承诺，将把国会批准的对乌克兰4亿美元军事援助中的几乎全部款项支出。
items.zhFull:
据三位了解该计划的消息人士称，特朗普政府已做出具有法律约束力的承诺，将把国会去年年底批准的4亿美元对乌军事援助资金几乎全部支出，确保这笔钱不会在9月30日到期作废。

消息人士称，截至本周初，乌克兰安全援助倡议（USAI）4亿美元资金中已有3.07亿美元完成拨付；这些要求匿名的消息人士表示，政府计划在9月30日本财年结束前锁定剩余的9300万美元。

负责监管USAI项目的五角大楼拒绝对此事置评。

首批交付包括武器和备件

这笔资金一直是与国会争执的焦点：民主党人和特朗普总统的一些共和党同僚批评五角大楼迟迟不发放对基辅的援助，而两党议员去年12月都投票支持了这笔援助。

近几个月，特朗普对乌克兰的语气更为积极，批准了一项允许乌克兰生产 Patriot 拦截导弹的提案，并签署了一项对俄制裁法案。

本周他在纽约联合国总部会见了乌克兰总统泽连斯基（Volodymyr Zelenskiy），会后泽连斯基表示，双方讨论了结束与俄罗斯战争的努力，包括可能就能源相关目标达成双边停火。

首批交付于本月开始，其中包括进攻性武器以及装甲车辆备件等装备。消息人士称，其余部分预计将在2029年10月前交付完毕。特朗普的白宫任期将于当年1月结束。

国会批准的这项一揽子计划中剩余的 9300 万美元无需在年底前支出，但如果届时未正式签订合同，这笔资金将失效。

未包含“爱国者”导弹

其中一名消息人士称，这批军事装备不包括“爱国者”导弹，尽管俄罗斯正用无人机和弹道导弹轰炸乌克兰的城市。

美国在伊朗的战争以及乌克兰战争已使全球“爱国者”导弹的库存消耗殆尽，基辅一直在恳求获得更多。

路透社 7 月报道称，该届政府已告知国会，这批装备可能需要数年时间才能送达乌克兰军队。由于担心美国武器库存过低，五角大楼已多次推迟向乌克兰运送武器。

议员们当时表示，他们对五角大楼的时间表感到不满，认为对于一场正在进行的冲突而言这一进度异常缓慢，该问题已在国会听证会上被反复提及。

自 2022 年 2 月俄罗斯发动全面入侵以来，乌克兰一直是美国对外援助的最大受援国，且远超其他国家和地区；但自特朗普（Trump）就职、其所属共和党于 2025 年 1 月控制国会两院以来，美国对基辅的承诺便受到质疑。

items.title: US appeals court upholds Pentagon’s blacklisting of Anthropic
items.author: Reuters
items.summary: A federal appeals court upheld the Pentagon’s blacklisting of Anthropic from military contracts, handing a victory to President Trump and the Pentagon.
items.body:
A federal appeals court on Friday upheld the Pentagon’s blacklisting of Anthropic from military contracts, handing a victory to President Donald Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth in their battle with the AI startup over safety guardrails on its technology.

The 2-1 decision by the U.S. Court of Appeals in Washington came in a lawsuit by Anthropic challenging its March designation by the Pentagon as a national security supply chain risk, which the startup says has cost it billions of dollars in lost business and damaged its reputation ahead of a highly anticipated initial public offering.

The court’s majority said it was reasonable for the Pentagon to designate Anthropic after it refused to allow its products to be used for autonomous weapons or mass surveillance. It rejected Anthropic’s claim that the Pentagon had retaliated against it for its views on AI safety and ethics.

Siding with Hegseth’s argument that Anthropic’s safety restrictions could compromise military operations, the majority said, “The Secretary raises the deeply sobering prospect of overly constrained AI models shutting down unexpectedly and thus causing important military operations to fail,” in an opinion by Judge Gregory Katsas.

San Francisco-based Anthropic said in a statement Friday that it respectfully disagrees with the decision but remains confident in its position and is considering its options, including review of the three-judge panel’s decision by the full appeals court.

The White House and the Department of Defense did not immediately respond to emails seeking comment.

A federal judge in San Francisco last month struck down a parallel designation under a different law, finding the administration had unlawfully retaliated against Anthropic for its views on AI safety. U.S. District Judge Rita Lin in San Francisco also blocked Trump’s government-wide ban on Anthropic and Hegseth’s order barring military contractors from doing any business with the startup.

Hegseth designated Anthropic as a risk under two different laws after Anthropic refused to remove guardrails against its technology being used for autonomous weapons or mass domestic surveillance.

The unprecedented move came after months of negotiations ended in failure and public recriminations by Hegseth and Trump, who accused Anthropic of endangering American lives with ideological posturing.

Anthropic denied that characterization and said AI is not yet reliable enough to be safely used in autonomous weapons. The company also said it opposes domestic surveillance as a violation of fundamental rights.
items.titleZh: 美国上诉法院维持五角大楼将Anthropic列入黑名单的决定
items.summaryZh: 一家联邦上诉法院维持了五角大楼将Anthropic列入黑名单、禁止其获得军事合同的决定，这成为特朗普总统和五角大楼的一次胜利。
items.zhFull:
周五，一家联邦上诉法院维持了五角大楼将Anthropic列入军事合同黑名单的决定，这使总统唐纳德·特朗普(Donald Trump)和国防部长皮特·海格塞斯(Pete Hegseth)在与这家AI初创公司就其技术安全护栏的争斗中获胜。

华盛顿的美国联邦上诉法院以2比1作出的这一裁决，源于Anthropic提起的诉讼，该公司质疑五角大楼在3月将其指定为国家安全供应链风险。这家初创公司称，这一指定使其损失了数十亿美元业务，并在备受期待的首次公开募股前损害了其声誉。

法院多数意见称，在Anthropic拒绝允许其产品被用于自主武器或大规模监控后，五角大楼将其指定为风险是合理的。法院驳回了Anthropic的说法，即五角大楼因其在AI安全与伦理方面的观点而对其实施报复。

多数意见支持海格塞斯的论点，即Anthropic的安全限制可能危及军事行动。在法官格雷戈里·卡察斯(Gregory Katsas)撰写的一份意见书中，多数意见称：“部长提出了一个令人深感警醒的前景：受到过度约束的AI模型意外关闭，从而导致重要军事行动失败。”

总部位于旧金山的Anthropic周五在一份声明中表示，它尊重但不同意该裁决，但对其立场仍抱有信心，并正在考虑各种选项，包括由全体上诉法院法官复审该三人法官合议庭的裁决。

白宫和国防部没有立即回应寻求置评的电子邮件。

上月，旧金山的一名联邦法官推翻了依据另一部法律作出的类似指定，认定政府因Anthropic在AI安全方面的观点而对其实施了非法报复。旧金山的美国地区法官丽塔·林(Rita Lin)还阻止了特朗普针对Anthropic的整个政府范围的禁令，以及海格塞斯禁止军事承包商与该初创公司开展任何业务的命令。

在Anthropic拒绝移除防止其技术被用于自主武器或大规模国内监控的护栏后，海格塞斯依据两部不同法律将其指定为风险。

这一史无前例的举动出台之前，长达数月的谈判以失败告终，赫格塞思（Hegseth）与特朗普还公开互相指责，他们指控Anthropic以意识形态作秀，危及美国人的生命。

Anthropic否认这一说法，并表示人工智能目前尚不够可靠，无法安全地用于自主武器。该公司还表示，反对国内监控，认为这侵犯了基本权利。
